recipes.name: Tom yum goong (hot and sour prawn soup)
recipes.description: A clear, fiercely aromatic broth made from fried prawn shells, lemongrass, galangal and makrut lime leaves, sharpened with lime and chilli and poured over just-cooked prawns and mushrooms.

ingredients.name: Raw king prawns, peeled weight
ingredients.prep: about 600 g shell-on; peel and devein, keeping the heads and shells

ingredients.name: Lemongrass stalks
ingredients.prep: bruised and cut into 5 cm lengths

ingredients.name: Evaporated milk, for the creamy nam khon style

steps.t: Peel and devein the prawns, keeping the heads and shells in a separate bowl. Pat the peeled prawns dry and keep them in the fridge while you make the stock.

Heat the oil in the saucepan over medium-high heat. Add the heads and shells and fry, stirring and pressing the heads with a spoon to squeeze out their juices, until they turn bright orange and smell toasty, 3–4 minutes.

Pour in the water, bring to the boil, then lower the heat and simmer for 15 minutes. Strain the stock through the sieve, pressing hard on the shells, and discard them. You should have about 1 litre of pale orange stock.

While the stock simmers, prepare the aromatics: trim the lemongrass, bash each stalk along its length with the pestle or the flat of a knife to release its oils and cut it into lengths; slice the galangal (no need to peel it), tear the lime leaves and crush the chillies.
Return the stock to the pan and bring it back to the boil. Add the lemongrass, galangal and lime leaves and simmer for 5 minutes, until the kitchen smells sharply citrusy.
Add the mushrooms and tomato and simmer for 2 minutes. Add the prawns and cook for 1½–2 minutes, just until they turn pink and curl into a loose C shape; a tight O means they are overcooked.

Take the pan off the heat before seasoning: boiling lime juice turns bitter. Stir in the fish sauce, chillies and lime juice, and the evaporated milk if you want the creamy style. Taste: it should be sour first, then salty and hot. Add more lime or fish sauce to balance.
Ladle into bowls and scatter with coriander. The lemongrass, galangal and lime leaves flavour the soup but are not eaten, so push them aside. Serve straight away with jasmine rice.

recipes.storage: Best eaten as soon as it is made. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 2 days; the prawns toughen a little on reheating.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Nam prik pao (roasted chilli jam) stirred in with the lime turns this into the deeper, red-tinged restaurant style; add 1–2 tablespoons.

recipes.name: Gaeng massaman neua (massaman beef curry)
recipes.description: A mild, rich curry with Persian and Indian roots: beef braised in coconut milk until it falls apart, with potatoes, roasted peanuts and a paste fragrant with cardamom, cinnamon, cloves and nutmeg, finished sweet, salty and sour.
equipment: Heavy casserole or large pot with a lid

steps.t: Soak the deseeded chillies in a bowl of just-boiled water for 15 minutes until soft and pliable. Meanwhile toast the coriander seeds, cumin and cloves in the dry frying pan over medium-low heat, shaking often, for 2–3 minutes until fragrant and a shade darker; tip onto a plate so they don't keep cooking.

In the same dry pan over medium heat, roast the shallots, garlic, lemongrass and galangal, turning, for 6–8 minutes until soft and charred in spots. Roasting the aromatics first is what gives massaman paste its mellow, smoky depth.

Grind the toasted spices to a powder. Blend or pound them with the drained chillies, the roasted aromatics, nutmeg, white pepper, salt and the shrimp paste, if using, adding 2–3 tablespoons of the chilli soaking water, until you have a thick, smooth, brick-red paste.

Spoon about 6 tablespoons of the thick cream off the top of one can of coconut milk and set it aside. Put the beef in the casserole with the rest of that can, the water, cinnamon, cardamom and bay leaves. Bring to a simmer, cover and cook over low heat, with just a few bubbles breaking, for 1½ hours until the beef is almost tender.

Heat the oil and the reserved coconut cream in the wok over medium heat until it bubbles and the oil begins to separate. Add the paste and fry, stirring constantly, for 5–6 minutes until it darkens, smells deeply toasty and the oil pools at the edges. Lower the heat if it catches.

Scrape the fried paste into the beef, then add the second can of coconut milk, the potatoes, onion and peanuts. Simmer uncovered, stirring now and then, for 25–30 minutes until the potatoes are tender, the beef breaks apart with a spoon and the sauce has thickened slightly.

Season with the tamarind, palm sugar and fish sauce, stir until the sugar melts and simmer for 5 minutes more. Taste: massaman should be gently sweet first, then salty, with a soft sourness behind. Adjust with more of any of the three.
Rest the curry off the heat for 10 minutes, fishing out the cinnamon stick and bay leaves. Serve with jasmine rice and, if you like, a quick cucumber pickle. It tastes even better the next day.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days, or freeze for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: About 4 tablespoons of a good store-bought massaman paste can replace the homemade paste; skip the salt and taste before adding all the fish sauce.
Chicken thighs or lamb shoulder are also traditional; chicken needs only 30 minutes of braising before the potatoes go in.

recipes.name: Gaeng phed ped yang (red curry with roast duck)
recipes.description: A royal-style red curry: crisp roast duck simmered briefly in coconut milk with a homemade red paste, pineapple, cherry tomatoes and Thai basil, so sweet fruit cuts through the rich meat.

ingredients.name: Makrut lime leaves (or the zest of 1 makrut lime)

steps.t: Heat the oven to 200 °C. Prick the duck skin all over with a skewer without piercing the meat, rub with the salt and five-spice and set skin side up on the rack over the roasting tin. Roast for 60 minutes, until the skin is deep brown and crisp, the meat is tender and the juices run clear. Rest for 10 minutes and pour the fat into a jar, keeping 1 tablespoon for the curry.

While the duck roasts, soak the chillies in just-boiled water for 15 minutes. Toast the coriander seeds, cumin and peppercorns in the dry frying pan over medium-low heat for 2 minutes until fragrant, then grind them to a powder.

Pound the paste in the mortar, hardest ingredients first: lemongrass, galangal and coriander root with the salt, then the lime leaves, drained chillies, shallots, garlic, ground spices and shrimp paste, if using. Keep pounding and scraping down for 10–15 minutes until smooth and red. A blender is fine: add 2–3 tablespoons of chilli water and blend until completely smooth.
Chop each duck leg through the bone into 3–4 pieces with the cleaver, or pull the meat off in large chunks, keeping the crisp skin on.

Spoon about 5 tablespoons of thick cream from the top of the coconut milk into the wok with the reserved duck fat. Heat over medium until it bubbles and the oil separates out ("cracks"), 3–4 minutes. Add the paste and fry, stirring, for 3–4 minutes until it smells intensely fragrant and the oil turns red.

Pour in the rest of the coconut milk and the stock, add the fish sauce, palm sugar and torn lime leaves and simmer for 3 minutes. Add the duck, pineapple, tomatoes and lychees, if using, and simmer gently for 5 minutes, just until the duck is hot through and the tomatoes soften but still hold their shape.

Taste: the curry should be rich and salty with a gentle sweetness and the sharpness of the fruit. Adjust with fish sauce or sugar. Turn off the heat, stir in the basil and sliced chilli and let the basil wilt for a few seconds.
Serve in a deep bowl with plenty of jasmine rice to soak up the sauce. Bones are part of the dish, so put out a plate for them.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days; the duck skin softens in the sauce.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Shortcut: buy a Chinese roast duck from a barbecue shop, chop it through the bone and skip step 1; use 3–4 tablespoons of store-bought red curry paste in place of the homemade paste.
Keep the leftover duck fat for frying potatoes or rice.

recipes.name: Pad kra pao gai (holy basil chicken with fried egg)
recipes.description: Bangkok's favourite one-plate lunch: hand-chopped chicken stir-fried hard with garlic, chillies and holy basil in a salty-sweet sauce, served over rice with a crisp-edged fried egg.

ingredients.name: Holy basil (kra pao) leaves, or Thai basil
Vegetable oil, for frying the eggs
Hot cooked jasmine rice (about 150 g raw)
Fish sauce with sliced chillies (prik nam pla), for the table

steps.t: Have the rice cooked and hot. Chop the chicken with a heavy knife or cleaver, folding and chopping for 2–3 minutes, until it is a coarse mince; hand-chopping gives a better, juicier texture than bought mince. Stir the sauce ingredients together in a cup.
Pound the garlic and chillies in the mortar to a coarse, wet paste, about 1 minute. If you have no mortar, chop them very finely together.

Fry the eggs Thai-style: heat the 100 ml oil in the wok over medium-high heat until a drop of egg white sizzles instantly (about 180 °C). Slide in one egg and spoon hot oil over the white for 1–2 minutes, until the edges are brown, frilly and crisp and the white has puffed but the yolk is still runny. Lift out with the slotted spoon and repeat.

Pour the frying oil into a heatproof bowl (it can be strained and reused) and wipe the wok. Heat the 2 tablespoons of fresh oil over high heat until it shimmers, add the garlic-chilli paste and stir for 15–20 seconds until fragrant but not browned. The chilli fumes are strong, so turn on the extractor.
Add the chicken and stir-fry, breaking it up, for 3–4 minutes until it is no longer pink anywhere. Add the beans, if using, after the first minute so they stay crisp.
Pour in the sauce and toss for about 1 minute until the chicken is glossy and dark and only a spoonful of sauce is left in the wok.
Take the wok off the heat, add the basil and toss for 15 seconds until it just wilts and smells peppery. Spoon over the rice, top each plate with a fried egg and serve with prik nam pla on the side.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Holy basil tastes peppery and clove-like; Thai basil is sweeter but works. Minced beef (pad kra pao neua) and prawns are also popular.

recipes.name: Pad see ew gai (wide noodles with chicken and Chinese broccoli)
recipes.description: Wide rice noodles stir-fried in a very hot wok with chicken, egg and Chinese broccoli in dark sweet soy until smoky and charred at the edges.
equipment: Wok or large heavy frying pan

ingredients.name: Wide flat rice noodles, dried (or 450 g fresh sen yai)
Light soy sauce, for the chicken
Dark sweet soy sauce (see ew dam)
White vinegar with sliced chillies (prik nam som)

steps.t: Soak dried noodles in hot tap water for 10–15 minutes until pliable but still firm, then drain well. If using fresh noodles, separate the strands with your fingers; warm them for 30 seconds in the microwave if they are stiff from the fridge.

Mix the chicken with the teaspoon of light soy. Cut the gai lan stems on the diagonal into thin slices and the leaves into 5 cm pieces. Stir the sauce ingredients together. Have everything next to the stove: this cooks in under 10 minutes.

Heat the wok over high heat until it just begins to smoke. Add 1½ tablespoons of oil and the garlic, stir for 10 seconds, then add the chicken and stir-fry for 2–3 minutes until white all the way through. Add the gai lan stems and toss for 1 minute.
Push everything to one side, add the remaining oil to the empty space and crack in the eggs. Let them set for 20 seconds, then break them up roughly and mix them in.

Add the noodles and the sauce. Toss to coat, then spread the noodles out and leave them for 30–45 seconds without stirring so they char and caramelise against the hot metal. Toss and repeat 3–4 times, for 2–3 minutes in all, until the noodles are tender, evenly dark and smoky in spots. If they stick or break, add a tablespoon of water.
Add the gai lan leaves and toss for 30 seconds until just wilted. Taste and add a splash more light soy if needed.

Serve straight away with chilli vinegar, chilli flakes, sugar and fish sauce on the table so everyone can season their plate. If your wok is small, cook in two batches: crowding makes the noodles steam and turn mushy.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Broccolini or ordinary broccoli can stand in for gai lan. Thin-sliced beef or firm tofu are common alternatives to chicken.

recipes.name: Som tam Thai (green papaya salad)
recipes.description: Shredded green papaya pounded with garlic, chillies, dried shrimp and peanuts and dressed with lime, fish sauce and palm sugar: crunchy, hot, sour, salty and sweet all at once. This is the Bangkok style; see the Lao version for the funkier original.
equipment: Large clay or wooden mortar and pestle (or a large bowl and rolling pin)

ingredients.name: Green (unripe) papaya
ingredients.prep: peeled, seeded and shredded into long thin strands

steps.t: Shred the papaya with a julienne peeler into long strands, or score the peeled papaya deeply lengthways with a knife and shave off the strands. Soak in iced water for 10 minutes to crisp up, then drain and shake dry.

Pound the garlic and chillies in the mortar to a coarse paste. Add the dried shrimp and half the peanuts and pound until broken into small pieces. Add the palm sugar and pound and stir until it dissolves into the paste.
Add the beans and bruise them lightly with the pestle, then add the tomatoes and lime wedges and press them so they release their juices. Pour in the fish sauce and lime juice.

Add the papaya. With the pestle in one hand and a large spoon in the other, pound lightly and turn the salad over for about 1 minute, so the papaya is bruised and soaks up the dressing but stays crunchy. Don't mash it.

Taste and balance: it should be sour and salty first, then sweet and hot. Pile onto a plate, scatter with the remaining peanuts and serve straight away with the cabbage wedges, sticky rice and grilled chicken (gai yang).

recipes.storage: Best eaten within 30 minutes of making; the papaya goes limp. Undressed shredded papaya keeps in the fridge for 2 days.
notes: No mortar? Bash the garlic, chillies and shrimp on a board with the side of a knife, then toss everything together in a large bowl and squeeze with clean hands.
Green papaya is sold in Asian grocers; a firm green mango or kohlrabi makes a reasonable stand-in.

recipes.name: Larb gai (Isan minced chicken salad)
recipes.description: Warm minced chicken tossed with lime, fish sauce, chilli, shallots and lots of mint, thickened with nutty toasted rice powder. Eaten with sticky rice and crisp raw vegetables.
equipment: Mortar and pestle or spice grinder

steps.t: Make the toasted rice powder (khao khua): toast the sticky rice in the dry wok over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, for 8–10 minutes until it is deep golden brown and smells like popcorn. Tip it out to cool, then grind it in the mortar or grinder to a coarse, sandy powder.

Put the chicken and water in the wok or a saucepan over medium heat. Stir and break it up continuously into fine crumbs for 5–6 minutes, until it is cooked through with no pink left and most of the liquid has gone; a little moisture should remain so the dressing clings. Larb is poached, not fried, so it stays tender.
Take the pan off the heat and let the chicken cool for 2 minutes so the herbs won't wilt. Season with the fish sauce, lime juice and chilli flakes (and the sugar, if using) and stir well.

Stir in the shallots and half the rice powder, then fold in the spring onions, mint and coriander. Taste: it should be sour, salty and hot, with a toasty crunch from the rice. Add more lime, fish sauce or chilli to taste.

Pile onto a plate, sprinkle with the rest of the rice powder and serve warm or at room temperature with the cabbage, cucumber, raw beans and steamed sticky rice. Use a cabbage leaf or a ball of rice to scoop it up.

recipes.storage: Best freshly made. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 1 day; the herbs darken.
notes: Toasted rice powder keeps for a month in a jar, so it is worth making a larger batch.
Larb is often eaten as the main dish of an Isan meal, alongside som tam and gai yang.

recipes.name: Khao niao mamuang (mango sticky rice)
recipes.description: Steamed sticky rice soaked in warm sweet-salty coconut milk, served with ripe mango and a spoonful of thick coconut cream. The rice needs to soak for at least 4 hours first.
equipment: Steamer with a lid (or a sieve set over a pot)

ingredients.name: Toasted sesame seeds or crisp yellow mung beans

steps.t: Rinse the rice in several changes of water until it runs nearly clear, then cover with cold water and soak for at least 4 hours or overnight. The grains are ready when one crushes easily between your fingers.

Drain the rice and spread it in an even layer on a piece of damp muslin in the steamer basket. Steam over rapidly boiling water, covered, for about 25 minutes, flipping the rice over in one piece halfway through. It is done when every grain is translucent and chewy with no chalky white centre.

While the rice steams, warm the coconut milk with the 75 g sugar, the salt and the pandan leaves, if using, over low heat, stirring until the sugar dissolves, about 5 minutes. Don't let it boil, or the coconut milk can split and turn oily. Keep it warm.

Tip the hot rice into a bowl, pour over two-thirds of the warm coconut milk and stir gently with a spatula to coat every grain. Cover and leave for 20–30 minutes; the rice drinks up the liquid and turns glossy and plump. Stir in the rest if it still looks dry.

For the topping, warm the coconut cream with the tablespoon of sugar and the pinch of salt over low heat. Stir in the cornflour mixture and simmer gently, stirring, for 1–2 minutes until it thickens to a pourable custard. Let it cool.
Peel the mangoes, slice the two cheeks off each side of the flat stone and cut them into thick slices.
Mound the rice on plates beside the mango, spoon the coconut topping over the rice and scatter with sesame seeds or mung beans, if using. Serve at room temperature, never fridge-cold.

recipes.storage: Best on the day it is made, kept covered at room temperature for up to 4 hours. Refrigerated sticky rice hardens: re-steam it for 5 minutes to soften. Cut mango keeps for 1 day in the fridge.
notes: Use Thai glutinous rice (khao niao); ordinary short-grain rice will not turn chewy and translucent.

recipes.name: Khao soi gai (Chiang Mai curry noodle soup)
recipes.description: Northern Thailand's signature bowl: egg noodles and tender chicken legs in a rich coconut curry broth scented with turmeric and cardamom, topped with a nest of crisp fried noodles and served with pickled mustard greens, shallots and lime.

ingredients.name: Cardamom pods (black if you can find them)
Chicken legs, bone-in and skinless
ingredients.prep: drumsticks and thighs, or thighs halved

ingredients.name: Egg noodles, for the crispy topping
Roasted chilli flakes fried in a little oil

steps.t: Soak the chillies in just-boiled water for 15 minutes. Toast the coriander seeds and cardamom seeds in the dry frying pan over medium-low heat for 2 minutes until fragrant, then grind them. In the same pan, char the shallots, garlic and ginger for 5–6 minutes until soft and blackened in spots.
Blend or pound the drained chillies, charred aromatics, ground spices, turmeric, curry powder and shrimp paste, if using, with 2–3 tablespoons of the soaking water to a smooth orange-red paste.

Make the crispy topping: boil the 30 g of noodles for 2 minutes, drain and pat them very dry. Heat the frying oil in the small saucepan to 180 °C and fry the noodles in small loose handfuls for about 1 minute until golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper.

Spoon about 5 tablespoons of thick cream off the top of the coconut milk. Heat it with the 2 tablespoons of oil in the large pot over medium heat until it bubbles and the oil separates, then add the paste and fry, stirring, for 4–5 minutes until it darkens and smells rich and toasty.

Add the chicken and turn it in the paste for 2 minutes. Pour in the rest of the coconut milk and the stock and add the fish sauce, soy sauce and palm sugar. Simmer gently, partly covered, for 30–35 minutes until the chicken is tender and pulls easily from the bone with no pink near it.
Meanwhile, cook the 250 g of noodles in a separate pan of boiling water for 3–4 minutes (or as the packet says), drain and divide between four deep bowls.

Taste the broth: it should be rich, gently salty and slightly sweet. Adjust with fish sauce or sugar. Ladle the chicken and plenty of broth over the noodles and top each bowl with a tangle of crispy noodles and some coriander and spring onion.
Serve with the pickled mustard greens, sliced shallots, lime wedges and chilli oil on the side, so everyone can add sourness, crunch and heat to their own bowl.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the curry within 2 hours and eat within 3 days. Keep the noodles and the crispy topping separate (the topping stays crisp for a day in an airtight jar).
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: About 4 tablespoons of red curry paste mixed with 1 tablespoon of curry powder and 1 teaspoon of turmeric is a fair shortcut for the paste.

recipes.name: Gai yang with nam jim jaew (Isan grilled chicken)
recipes.description: A spatchcocked chicken marinated in garlic, coriander root, white pepper and lemongrass, grilled slowly until the skin is lacquered and smoky, then served with jaew, a sour and smoky chilli dipping sauce.
equipment: Barbecue with a lid (or oven and roasting tin with rack)

ingredients.name: Sticky rice, for toasted rice powder

steps.t: Spatchcock the chicken: with the breast down, cut along both sides of the backbone with the scissors and remove it. Turn the bird over and press firmly on the breastbone until it lies flat. Make two deep slashes in each thigh and drumstick so the marinade and heat get in.

Pound the garlic, coriander root, peppercorns and lemongrass in the mortar to a coarse paste. Stir in the fish sauce, soy sauce, palm sugar and oil. Rub it all over the chicken, under the breast skin and into the cuts. Cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 2 hours, or overnight.

For the jaew, toast the sticky rice in a dry pan over medium-low heat, stirring, for 6–8 minutes until deep golden, then grind it coarsely. Stir the fish sauce, lime juice, tamarind and palm sugar together until the sugar dissolves. Just before serving, add the chilli flakes, a tablespoon of the rice powder, the shallot and herbs.

Set up the barbecue for indirect medium heat, about 180 °C under the lid, with the coals banked to one side. Lay the chicken skin side up on the side away from the coals, close the lid and cook for 35–40 minutes, turning and moving it every 10 minutes so it colours evenly. It is ready when the thickest part of the thigh reads 74 °C.
Move the chicken over the coals, skin side down, for the last 3–5 minutes to crisp and char the skin. Watch it closely: the sugar in the marinade can flare and burn.
Rest the chicken for 10 minutes, then chop it through the bone with the cleaver into serving pieces. Serve with the jaew for dipping, steamed sticky rice and som tam.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: No barbecue? Roast on a rack in a 200 °C oven for 45–50 minutes, then grill under high heat for 3–4 minutes to crisp the skin.
Bone-in chicken legs work well too and take about 30 minutes.

recipes.name: Pla tod khamin (Southern turmeric fried fish)
recipes.description: A Southern Thai favourite: fish rubbed with turmeric, garlic and pepper, shallow-fried until crisp and golden, and showered with crunchy fried garlic. Simple, fragrant and good with rice and a sharp chilli dip.

ingredients.name: Mackerel fillets, skin on (or small whole fish, cleaned)
Ground turmeric (or 30 g fresh turmeric, peeled)
Fish sauce with sliced bird's eye chillies (nam pla prik)

steps.t: Pat the fish completely dry with kitchen paper and cut 3 shallow diagonal slashes in the skin of each fillet (or deeper ones on both sides of whole fish). Dry fish fries crisp; wet fish spits and steams.

Pound the turmeric (fresh or ground), the 6 marinade cloves of garlic, white pepper and salt in the mortar to a damp yellow paste. Rub it all over the fish and into the slashes. Leave for 15–30 minutes while you prepare everything else.
Crush the 8 unpeeled garlic cloves in the mortar into rough chunks, skins and all; the papery skins crisp up too.

Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat to about 175 °C, when a pinch of the turmeric paste sizzles vigorously. Lay the fish in skin side down, away from you, and fry without moving for 4–5 minutes until the skin is deep golden and crisp. Turn carefully and fry for 3–4 minutes more, until the flesh is opaque and flakes easily. Drain on the rack.

Lower the heat to medium and fry the crushed garlic in the same oil, stirring, for 2–3 minutes until golden and crisp. Lift it out the moment it turns golden, as it goes bitter within seconds, and drain on paper.
Pile the fried garlic over the fish and serve hot with jasmine rice, sliced cucumber, lime wedges and nam pla prik for dipping.

recipes.storage: Best eaten hot and crisp. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a hot oven (200 °C) for 8–10 minutes until steaming hot, which keeps the skin crisp.
notes: Sea bass, snapper or kingfish steaks work equally well; adjust the frying time to the thickness.

recipes.name: Cha yen (Thai iced tea)
recipes.description: Strong, spiced Thai tea sweetened with sugar and condensed milk, poured over crushed ice and crowned with a swirl of evaporated milk.
equipment: Tea sock or fine sieve lined with muslin

ingredients.name: Thai tea mix (cha tra mue), or strong loose black tea
Star anise, if using plain black tea

steps.t: Bring the water to the boil, take it off the heat and add the tea (and the star anise if you are using plain black tea). Steep for 5 minutes, stirring once; Thai tea needs to be very strong to stand up to the milk and ice.
Strain through the tea sock or a muslin-lined sieve into a jug, pressing on the leaves. For a deeper colour, pour the tea back through the leaves once more.
While the tea is hot, stir in the sugar and condensed milk until completely dissolved. Leave to cool for 10 minutes, or chill it if you have time, so it doesn't melt all the ice at once.

Fill the glasses to the top with crushed ice and pour in the tea until they are three-quarters full. Spoon the evaporated milk over the top so it trickles down in orange-and-cream swirls, and stir just before drinking.

recipes.storage: The sweetened tea keeps in a covered jug in the fridge for 3 days; add ice and evaporated milk to serve.
notes: Thai tea mix is a blend of black tea with spices and usually food colouring, which gives the famous orange colour; plain black tea tastes similar but looks brown.

recipes.name: Larb neua (Lao beef larb)
recipes.description: Laos's national dish in its beef version: hand-chopped beef cooked in its own juices, then tossed with padaek and lime, toasted rice and shaved galangal, and a big tangle of mint, sawtooth coriander and spring onion.

ingredients.name: Galangal, for toasting with the rice
Lean beef steak (sirloin, rump or flank)
Padaek (Lao fermented fish sauce), strained, or extra fish sauce

steps.t: Toast the sticky rice with the sliced galangal in a dry wok over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, for 8–10 minutes until the rice is deep golden and smells nutty. Cool, then pound to a coarse powder (the galangal adds a gentle perfume).
Chop the beef by hand: slice it thinly, then chop and fold it with a heavy knife for 3–4 minutes into a coarse mince. Hand-chopped beef keeps its juices and gives larb its texture.
Put the beef and water in the wok over medium heat and stir, breaking it up, for 4–5 minutes, until no pink remains and the juices have mostly cooked away. Tip into a bowl and leave for 2 minutes.

Season the warm beef with the padaek, fish sauce, lime juice and chilli flakes, then mix in the chopped galangal, lemongrass, shallots and two-thirds of the rice powder. Lao larb is less sweet than Thai versions and more savoury and herbal, with a bitter, peppery edge from the galangal.

Fold in the spring onions, mint, sawtooth coriander and dill, if using, and taste for salt, sour and heat. Scatter with the remaining rice powder and serve with lettuce, raw beans and cucumber, and plenty of steamed sticky rice.

recipes.storage: Best freshly made. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 1 day.
notes: In Laos larb is also made with duck, chicken or fish; it is the centre of the meal rather than a side salad.
Padaek is thicker and funkier than Thai fish sauce; strain off the liquid and discard the solids.

recipes.name: Tam mak hoong (Lao papaya salad)
recipes.description: The Lao original of papaya salad: thick strands of green papaya pounded hard with garlic, plenty of chilli, tomatoes and lime, and seasoned with pungent padaek instead of the peanuts and sugar of the Bangkok style.
equipment: Large clay or wooden mortar and pestle

ingredients.name: Green (unripe) papaya
ingredients.prep: peeled, seeded and cut into thick strands

steps.t: Cut the papaya the Lao way: hold the peeled papaya in one hand and chop into it with a heavy knife to make many parallel cuts, then shave the strands off with a peeler or the knife. Lao strands are thicker and crunchier than the fine Thai shreds.
Pound the garlic and chillies in the mortar to a coarse paste. Lao tam is hot, so use as many chillies as you dare. Add the palm sugar and the shrimp paste, if using, and pound to combine.
Add the tomatoes and pound to burst them, then add the padaek, fish sauce and lime juice and stir with a spoon to mix the dressing.

Add the papaya and pound firmly while turning it over with a spoon for 1–2 minutes, harder than for the Thai version, until the strands are well bruised, darkened by the dressing and slightly softened.
Taste: it should be salty, sour, funky and hot, with only a hint of sweetness. Serve straight away with cabbage, raw beans, sticky rice and grilled meat or larb.

recipes.storage: Best eaten within 30 minutes of making; the papaya softens and weeps as it sits.
notes: Padaek gives the salad its deep, fermented flavour; with fish sauce alone it is milder but still good.

recipes.name: Khao piak sen (Lao chicken noodle soup)
recipes.description: Laos's comfort soup: thick, chewy hand-cut rice and tapioca noodles cooked straight in a gingery chicken broth, which turns silky as they release their starch, finished with garlic oil, herbs and lime.

ingredients.name: Tapioca starch, plus extra for dusting

steps.t: Put the chicken and water in the stock pot and bring slowly to the boil, skimming off the grey foam as it rises so the broth stays clear. Add the lemongrass, galangal, charred shallots and garlic and coriander roots, lower the heat and simmer very gently for 45 minutes.
Lift out the chicken, pull the meat off the bones in shreds and set it aside. Strain the broth into a clean pan (you need about 2 litres) and season it with the fish sauce, salt and sugar.

While the broth simmers, make the dough: mix the rice flour, tapioca starch and salt in the bowl, pour in the boiling water a little at a time while stirring with chopsticks, then knead with your hands once it is cool enough, 4–5 minutes, until smooth, soft and pliable like modelling clay. Add a spoonful of flour if it is sticky. Cover and rest for 10 minutes.
Roll the dough out on a surface dusted with tapioca starch to about 3 mm thick. Cut it into strips about 5 mm wide and toss them with more starch so they don't stick together.
For the garlic oil, fry the chopped garlic in the oil in the small pan over medium-low heat, stirring, for 3–4 minutes until pale golden and crisp. Tip into a bowl straight away.

Bring the broth to a rolling boil. Shake the excess starch off the noodles and drop them in, stirring so they don't clump. Cook for 5–6 minutes, until they turn translucent, float and are chewy-tender; the starch thickens the broth to a silky body.
Return the chicken to the pot to heat through, then ladle into bowls. Top with garlic oil, spring onions and coriander and serve with bean sprouts, lime wedges and chilli on the side.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days. The noodles keep absorbing broth, so add a splash of water when reheating.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Tapioca starch gives the noodles their bounce; cornflour is not a good substitute.

recipes.name: Khao niao (Lao steamed sticky rice)
recipes.description: The everyday rice of Laos and northeastern Thailand: soaked glutinous rice steamed until chewy and translucent, then eaten with the fingers to scoop up larb, jaew and grilled meats.
equipment: Bamboo steaming basket and pot, or a steamer lined with muslin
Basket or cloth-lined bowl with a lid

steps.t: Rinse the rice in several changes of water, then cover with plenty of cold water and soak for at least 4 hours, or overnight. Properly soaked grains are opaque white and crush easily between your fingers.

Bring about 5 cm of water to the boil in the pot. Drain the rice, put it in the bamboo basket or muslin-lined steamer and set it over the boiling water without letting the rice touch the water. Cover and steam for 15 minutes.

Flip the rice over in one piece (toss it in the basket, or turn it with a spatula), cover again and steam for 10–15 minutes more, until every grain is translucent, glossy and chewy with no hard centre.

Turn the rice out onto a board or tray and spread and fold it with the spatula for a minute to let the steam escape; this keeps it from turning mushy. Pack it loosely into a covered basket or a bowl lined with a cloth. To eat, pinch off a walnut-sized piece and roll it into a ball with your fingers.

recipes.storage: Keep covered at room temperature for up to 4 hours. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours for up to 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Re-steam refrigerated sticky rice for 5–10 minutes until soft and steaming hot.
notes: Sticky rice must be steamed, not boiled; boiling turns it into a paste.

recipes.name: Phở bò Hà Nội (Hanoi beef pho)
recipes.description: Hanoi's beef noodle soup: a long-simmered, crystal-clear broth scented with charred onion, ginger, star anise and cinnamon, poured boiling over rice noodles, tender brisket and paper-thin slices of raw beef that cook in the bowl.
equipment: Very large stock pot (at least 8 litres)

ingredients.name: Beef bones with some meat (knuckle, marrow bones or oxtail), or bone-in short ribs
Beef brisket or flank, in one piece
Beef sirloin or eye of round, for raw slices
Onion
ingredients.prep: sliced paper-thin and soaked in cold water

ingredients.name: Rice vinegar with sliced garlic (giấm tỏi)

steps.t: Put the bones and brisket in the pot, cover with cold water and bring to a hard boil for 10 minutes. Drain into the sink, rinse the bones and meat under running water and scrub the pot clean. This first blanching removes the scum and blood and is the secret to a clear broth.
Char the onion halves and ginger directly over a gas flame with tongs, or under a very hot grill, turning, until blackened in patches, 8–10 minutes. Rinse off loose burnt bits and peel the onions.

Return the bones and brisket to the clean pot with the 4.5 litres of water and the charred onion and ginger. Bring slowly to a bare simmer, skimming off any foam, and keep it there, uncovered, with just a few bubbles breaking: boiling hard makes the broth cloudy and greasy.

After about 1½ hours, when a skewer slides easily into the brisket, lift it out, plunge it into cold water for 10 minutes to stop it darkening, then wrap and refrigerate. Keep the bones simmering for another 3 hours, topping up with hot water to keep them covered.

Toast the star anise, cinnamon, cloves, cardamom, coriander and fennel in a dry pan over medium heat for 2 minutes until fragrant, tie them in the spice bag and add to the pot for the last 45 minutes only; longer and the spices turn bitter.

Strain the broth through the fine sieve into a clean pan, skim off as much fat as you can and season with the fish sauce, sugar and salt. You should have about 3 litres of deep golden, well-seasoned broth. Keep it at a rolling boil for serving.

Freeze the sirloin for 20 minutes to firm it, then slice it as thinly as you can across the grain. Slice the cold brisket thinly too. Soak the noodles in warm water for 20 minutes, then dunk them in boiling water for 30–60 seconds until just tender and drain.

Divide the noodles between six large, warmed bowls. Top with brisket, raw beef, onion slices, spring onion and coriander, then ladle over the boiling broth so it cooks the raw beef pink. In Hanoi pho comes with lime, chilli and garlic vinegar; the plate of basil and bean sprouts is a Southern habit.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the broth within 2 hours for up to 4 days (lift off the set fat before reheating), or freeze it for 3 months. Keep meat and noodles separate.
recipes.reheating: Bring the broth back to a rolling boil before ladling it over the bowls.
safety: The raw beef slices are cooked only by the boiling broth: pour it straight from a rolling boil, and use cooked brisket only for anyone pregnant, very young, elderly or unwell.
notes: Ask the butcher for knuckle and marrow bones with some meat attached; oxtail gives a richer, gelatinous broth.

recipes.name: Bún bò Nam Bộ (lemongrass beef noodle salad)
recipes.description: A Hanoi favourite despite its "southern" name: rice vermicelli piled with herbs and lettuce, hot lemongrass-seared beef, pickles, fried shallots and peanuts, all tossed with sweet-sour nước chấm at the table.

ingredients.name: Vegetable oil, for frying the shallots

steps.t: Toss the beef with the lemongrass, garlic, fish sauce, sugar, pepper and 1 tablespoon of the oil and leave to marinate for 20 minutes while you prepare everything else.

Mix the carrot and daikon with the vinegar, sugar and a pinch of salt and leave for at least 15 minutes, until softened and sweet-sour. For the nước chấm, stir the sugar into the warm water until dissolved, then add the fish sauce, lime juice, garlic and chilli. Taste: it should be light, sweet, sour and salty in balance, a sauce to pour rather than a strong dip.

Fry the shallots in the 3 tablespoons of oil in the small frying pan over medium-low heat, stirring often, for 6–8 minutes until evenly golden. Lift them onto kitchen paper (they crisp as they cool) and keep the fragrant oil.

Cook the vermicelli in a large pan of boiling water for 4–5 minutes, until soft but springy, then rinse under cold water, drain very well and leave to dry for a few minutes so it doesn't water down the bowls.
Divide the lettuce, bean sprouts, cucumber and herbs between four large bowls and pile the noodles on top. Drain the pickles.

Heat the wok over high heat until smoking, add the remaining tablespoon of oil and the onion and stir-fry for 1 minute. Add the beef in one layer, leave it for 30 seconds to sear, then toss for 1–2 minutes more until just browned with a little pink left. Work in two batches if your wok is small, or the beef will stew.

Spoon the hot beef and its juices over the noodles and top with pickles, peanuts, fried shallots and a drizzle of shallot oil. Pour 3–4 tablespoons of nước chấm over each bowl at the table and toss everything together before eating.

recipes.storage: Store components separately in the fridge and eat within 2 days; the beef is best freshly cooked.
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Gỏi cuốn tôm (prawn summer rolls)
recipes.description: Fresh rice-paper rolls packed with poached prawns, vermicelli, crisp lettuce and herbs, served with a warm hoisin and peanut dipping sauce.

steps.t: Bring a saucepan of salted water to the boil, add the prawns and simmer for 2 minutes until pink and just firm. Drain and cool in iced water, then peel, devein and slice each one in half lengthways into two thin halves.

Cook the vermicelli in boiling water for 3–4 minutes until soft, rinse under cold water and drain thoroughly. Lay out the lettuce, herbs, chives, noodles and prawns in separate piles around a clean board.

For the sauce, warm the oil in the small pan over medium heat and fry the garlic for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the hoisin, peanut butter and water and stir for 1–2 minutes until smooth and glossy. Pour into small bowls and top with crushed peanuts and chilli sauce, if using.
Fill the shallow dish with warm water. Dip one rice paper in for 2–3 seconds, just until it is pliable but still slightly firm (it keeps softening), and lay it flat on the damp towel or board.

Lay a piece of lettuce, a small bundle of noodles and some herbs across the lower third of the wrapper. Place three prawn halves, pink side down, in a row just above. Fold the bottom edge over the filling, fold in both sides, then roll up firmly, tucking a chive stem in at the last turn so it sticks out of one end. Repeat with the rest.
Keep the finished rolls under a damp tea towel so they don't dry out, and serve within 2 hours with the dipping sauce.

recipes.storage: Best eaten within 2 hours, covered with a damp towel at cool room temperature. In the fridge the wrappers harden; wrap rolls individually and eat within 1 day.
notes: Don't over-soak the wrappers: limp ones tear. If a wrapper splits, roll a second one around it.

recipes.name: Bò kho (Vietnamese lemongrass beef stew)
recipes.description: Beef braised slowly with lemongrass, star anise, cinnamon and tomato in coconut water until meltingly tender, with sweet carrots. A Saigon breakfast or supper, eaten with crusty bánh mì for dunking.
equipment: Heavy casserole or large pot with a lid

ingredients.name: Annatto seeds or sweet paprika, for colour
Lemongrass stalks
ingredients.prep: bruised and tied in a knot

steps.t: Mix the beef with the minced lemongrass, garlic, shallots, ginger, five-spice, fish sauce, sugar and pepper in the bowl. Cover and marinate for at least 1 hour in the fridge, or overnight for deeper flavour.

Heat the oil in the casserole over medium heat and add the annatto seeds; stir for 1–2 minutes until the oil turns deep orange, then scoop out and discard the seeds. (If using paprika, stir it in with the beef instead so it doesn't burn.)

Turn the heat to high and brown the beef in two batches, letting the pieces sit for 2 minutes before turning, until seared on most sides, about 6 minutes per batch. Scrape the marinade in with the last batch.

Return all the beef to the pot, stir in the tomato paste and cook for 1 minute, then add the knotted lemongrass, star anise, cinnamon, coconut water and water. Bring to the boil, skim off any foam, cover and simmer over low heat for 1½ hours, stirring occasionally.

Add the carrots and simmer, partly covered, for 30–40 minutes more, until the beef breaks apart with a spoon, the carrots are tender and the sauce has reduced to a light, glossy gravy. Add a splash of water if it reduces too far.
Fish out the lemongrass, star anise and cinnamon. Taste and adjust with fish sauce or a pinch of sugar: it should be savoury and gently sweet, with warm spice.
Ladle into bowls, scatter with basil and serve with warm baguettes to tear and dunk, and lime and chilli on the side. Bò kho is also good over rice noodles or with rice.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days, or freeze for up to 3 months. The flavour improves overnight.
recipes.reheating: @reheat

recipes.name: Cá kho tộ (caramelised catfish in a clay pot)
recipes.description: Mekong Delta home cooking: catfish steaks simmered in a dark caramel, fish sauce and coconut water with lots of black pepper until sticky, salty-sweet and glazed. Served with rice and a sour soup.
equipment: Clay pot or small heavy saucepan with a lid

ingredients.name: Catfish or basa steaks, 2.5 cm thick (bone-in or fillet)
Black pepper, coarsely ground, plus extra to finish

steps.t: Make the caramel (nước màu): heat the sugar and water in the small saucepan over medium heat without stirring, swirling the pan gently, for 5–7 minutes. Watch closely as it turns golden, then amber, then the colour of strong tea. Take it off the heat the moment it smells bittersweet and pour in 3 tablespoons of hot water at arm's length; it will spit. Stir until smooth.
Pat the fish dry and put it in a bowl with the fish sauce, brown sugar, pepper, half the shallots and garlic and 2 tablespoons of the caramel. Turn to coat and marinate for 15–30 minutes.
Heat the oil in the clay pot over medium heat and fry the remaining shallots and garlic for 1 minute until fragrant and golden.

Lay the fish in the pot in a single layer, pour over the marinade, the rest of the caramel and enough coconut water to come halfway up the fish. Bring to the boil, then cover, lower the heat and simmer gently for 20 minutes, turning the steaks once.

Uncover and simmer for 10–15 minutes more, basting the fish with the sauce, until the liquid has reduced to a dark, syrupy glaze that coats the fish and the flesh flakes easily. Don't stir, or the fish will break.

Scatter over the chilli, spring onions and a generous grinding of black pepper and cook for 1 minute more. Serve straight from the pot with plenty of steamed rice, a bowl of canh chua or plain boiled vegetables to balance the intense, salty sauce.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days; the glaze firms up when cold and loosens again when warmed.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: The caramel can be made in a larger batch and kept in a jar for months; Vietnamese cooks use it in many braises.

recipes.name: Bún bò Huế (spicy lemongrass beef noodle soup)
recipes.description: The imperial city's fiery noodle soup: a beef broth heavy with lemongrass and fermented shrimp paste, red with chilli and annatto oil, poured over thick round rice noodles and sliced shank, with a big plate of herbs.

ingredients.name: Beef shank, in one or two pieces
Thick round rice noodles (bún bò Huế), dried

steps.t: Put the shank and brisket in the stock pot, cover with cold water, boil hard for 5 minutes, then drain and rinse the meat and pot. This keeps the broth clean.

Return the meat to the pot with the 4 litres of water, the lemongrass bundles and onion. Bring to a gentle simmer, skimming off the foam, and cook uncovered, barely bubbling, for 2 hours, until the shank is tender but still holds its shape. Lift the meat out into a bowl of cold water for 10 minutes, then drain and refrigerate.

Stir the shrimp paste into 250 ml of cold water and leave it to settle for 10 minutes. Pour only the cloudy liquid into the broth, leaving the gritty sediment behind. Simmer the broth for another 30 minutes, then strain it, skim off some of the fat and season with the fish sauce, sugar and salt.

For the sa tế, heat the oil with the annatto seeds in the small saucepan over medium heat for 1–2 minutes until deep red, then strain out the seeds (or add the paprika with the chilli). Add the minced lemongrass, garlic and shallots and fry gently for 3–4 minutes until golden, then stir in the chilli flakes off the heat. Stir half into the broth and keep the rest for the table.
Soak the noodles in warm water for 30 minutes, then boil for 8–10 minutes until soft and slippery but still bouncy. Drain and rinse with hot water.

Slice the shank and brisket thinly across the grain. Bring the broth back to a rolling boil and taste: it should be salty, spicy and strongly perfumed with lemongrass, with a deep savoury undertone from the shrimp paste.

Divide the noodles between six deep bowls, top with the sliced beef, onion, spring onion and coriander, and ladle over the boiling broth. Serve with the herb plate, lime wedges and the rest of the chilli oil so everyone can adjust the heat.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the broth within 2 hours for up to 4 days, or freeze for 3 months. Store meat, noodles and herbs separately.
recipes.reheating: Bring the broth to a rolling boil before ladling over the noodles and meat.
notes: In Hue the soup traditionally includes pork hock and pork sausage; this beef-only version is common and halal-friendly.
Mắm ruốc is pungent; start with 1 tablespoon if you are new to it.

recipes.name: Bánh xèo (sizzling crêpes with prawns)
recipes.description: Lacy, crisp turmeric-yellow rice-flour crêpes, named for the sizzle of batter hitting the pan, filled with prawns, mung beans and bean sprouts and eaten wrapped in lettuce and herbs with nước chấm.
equipment: Non-stick frying pan, 25 cm, with a lid

steps.t: Whisk the rice flour, cornflour, turmeric and salt with the coconut milk and cold water to a smooth batter as thin as single cream. Stir in the spring onions and leave to rest for at least 30 minutes; resting hydrates the flour and gives a crisper crêpe.

Drain the mung beans and steam or simmer them in a little water for 10–12 minutes until soft but still holding their shape. Drain well. For the nước chấm, stir the sugar into the warm water until dissolved, then add the fish sauce, lime juice, garlic and chilli. Taste: it should be light, sweet, sour and salty in balance, a sauce to pour rather than a strong dip.
Heat 1½ teaspoons of oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat. Add a few slices of onion and 6–8 prawn pieces (and pork, if using) and fry for 1 minute until the prawns start to turn pink.

Stir the batter, then pour in a small ladleful (about 100 ml) while tilting and swirling the pan so it runs up the sides in a thin, lacy layer. It should sizzle loudly. Scatter a spoonful of mung beans and a handful of bean sprouts over one half, cover and cook for 2 minutes until the sprouts wilt.

Uncover, drizzle about ¾ teaspoon of oil around the edge and cook for 3–4 minutes more, until the underside is golden and crisp and the crêpe releases easily from the pan. Fold it in half like an omelette and slide onto a plate.
Repeat with the remaining batter and filling to make 8 crêpes, stirring the batter each time as the flour settles. Keep the finished ones on a rack in a low oven so they stay crisp.
To eat, tear off a piece of crêpe, wrap it in a lettuce leaf with some herbs and dip it in the nước chấm. Bánh xèo is best eaten as it comes out of the pan.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away. Refrigerate leftover crêpes within 2 hours and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a dry frying pan over medium heat for 2–3 minutes per side until sizzling and hot through.
notes: The first crêpe is often a test: if it is thick and soft, thin the batter with a little water; if it breaks, let the pan get hotter.

recipes.name: Cà phê sữa đá (Vietnamese iced coffee)
recipes.description: Strong dark-roast coffee dripped slowly through a phin filter onto sweetened condensed milk, stirred and poured over ice.
equipment: Vietnamese phin filter (or a cafetière or moka pot)

ingredients.name: Strong coffee (from about 4 tbsp dark-roast ground coffee)

steps.t: Spoon 2 tablespoons of condensed milk into the bottom of each heatproof glass. Boil the kettle and let it stand for 30 seconds so the water is just off the boil.

Put 2 tablespoons of medium-coarse ground coffee in the phin, shake it level and set the press on top. Place the phin on the first glass, pour in about 20 ml of hot water and wait 30 seconds while the coffee swells and blooms.

Fill the phin with hot water, cover with the lid and let it drip slowly for 4–5 minutes; if it runs through in under 2 minutes, press the screen down a little more next time. Repeat for the second glass.
Stir the coffee into the condensed milk until evenly caramel-coloured, then pour over glasses packed with ice and stir again. Drink while ice-cold.

recipes.storage: Best made fresh. Brewed coffee and condensed milk keep, mixed and covered, for 2 days in the fridge.
notes: Leave out the ice and drink it hot for cà phê sữa nóng.
Vietnamese coffee is traditionally robusta, often roasted with a little butter; any strong dark roast works.

recipes.name: Chè chuối (banana and tapioca in coconut milk)
recipes.description: A warm Southern Vietnamese sweet soup: ripe bananas and chewy tapioca pearls simmered in salted coconut milk, topped with crushed roasted peanuts and toasted sesame.

ingredients.name: Ripe bananas, small Asian or ordinary (about 5)

steps.t: Cut the bananas into 3–4 cm chunks on the diagonal (leave small Asian bananas whole if you like) and toss them with 2 tablespoons of the sugar and the salt. Leave for 10–15 minutes: the sugar draws out moisture and the bananas turn slightly rosy and firm, so they hold their shape when cooked.
Toast the sesame seeds in the dry frying pan over medium-low heat, shaking, for 2–3 minutes until golden and fragrant. Tip onto a plate.

Bring the water to the boil in the saucepan with the pandan, if using. Drain the tapioca and add it, stirring so the pearls don't clump, and simmer for 6–8 minutes until they are almost completely translucent with a tiny white dot in the centre.

Pour in the coconut milk and the rest of the sugar and bring back to a gentle simmer, stirring. Add the bananas with any syrup and cook over low heat for 5–7 minutes, stirring gently now and then, until the bananas are soft and the tapioca is fully clear. Don't let it boil hard, or the coconut milk turns oily.
Take out the pandan leaves. Taste: it should be sweet with a distinctly salty edge, which is what makes the coconut taste rich. The chè thickens as it cools; loosen it with a little water if needed.
Ladle into small bowls and scatter with the peanuts and sesame. Serve warm, or at room temperature on a hot day.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 2 days; the tapioca firms up when cold.
recipes.reheating: Warm gently over low heat with a splash of water, stirring, until hot.
notes: Ripe but firm bananas work best; very soft ones fall apart.

recipes.name: Xôi xéo (Hanoi turmeric sticky rice with mung bean and crispy shallots)
recipes.description: Hanoi's street breakfast: golden turmeric sticky rice topped with thin shavings of seasoned mung bean paste, crisp fried shallots and a drizzle of fragrant shallot oil. The rice and beans need soaking the night before.
equipment: Steamer with a lid, lined with muslin

steps.t: The night before, rinse the sticky rice and soak it in cold water with the turmeric stirred in. Rinse and soak the mung beans separately. Both need at least 4 hours; overnight is best.

Drain the rice, mix in the teaspoon of salt and spread it on the muslin in the steamer. Steam over rapidly boiling water, covered, for 30–35 minutes, turning the rice over halfway, until the grains are glossy, translucent and chewy all the way through.

Meanwhile, drain the mung beans and steam them alongside, or simmer them in just enough water to cover for 15–20 minutes, until soft and crumbly and the water is absorbed. Mash with the half-teaspoon of salt to a smooth, thick paste while hot.

Press the warm mung bean paste firmly into a tight ball or log with your hands; it should hold together like soft clay. Leave it to cool and firm for 10 minutes, then shave off thin slices with a sharp knife (xéo means 'sliced at an angle').

Fry the shallots in the oil in the frying pan over medium heat, stirring often, for 8–10 minutes until evenly deep golden. Pour through the sieve set over a bowl, keeping the oil, and spread the shallots on kitchen paper; they crisp up as they cool. Take them out just before they look done, as they keep colouring.
Toss the hot rice with 2 tablespoons of the shallot oil to give it a sheen.

To serve, pack a portion of rice into a bowl or onto a square of banana leaf, cover with mung bean shavings, spoon over a little more shallot oil and finish with a big pinch of crispy shallots. Eat warm.

recipes.storage: Keep covered at room temperature for up to 4 hours. Refrigerate leftover rice within 2 hours for up to 2 days; keep the shallots in an airtight jar for a week.
recipes.reheating: Re-steam refrigerated rice for 5–10 minutes until soft and steaming hot.
notes: Street vendors often add chicken floss or a fried egg; leftover shallot oil is wonderful on noodles and rice.

recipes.name: Rau muống xào tỏi (water spinach with garlic)
recipes.description: The everyday green of a Vietnamese meal: hollow-stemmed water spinach blanched, then flash-fried with lots of golden garlic until bright and crunchy.

steps.t: Snap or cut the water spinach into 8–10 cm lengths, discarding the tough lower stems. Split very thick stems lengthways so they cook evenly. Wash well in plenty of water and drain.

Bring a large pan of well-salted water to a rolling boil. Blanch the water spinach for 30–45 seconds, just until the stems turn bright green, then plunge it into the iced water to stop the cooking and keep the colour. Drain and squeeze gently.

Heat the oil in the wok over medium heat and fry half the garlic for about 1 minute until pale golden and fragrant. Turn the heat to high, add the water spinach, salt and sugar and toss for 1–2 minutes until hot through and glossy, with the stems still crunchy.

Add the rest of the garlic and the fish sauce, if using, toss for 15 seconds and serve straight away with rice, alongside a braise such as cá kho tộ. In Hanoi the blanching water is often served too, soured with a squeeze of lime, as a simple soup.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away; leftovers turn dark. Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 1 day.
notes: Morning glory, kangkung and ong choy are all names for water spinach. Ordinary spinach works but needs no blanching.

recipes.name: Nasi lemak with sambal ikan bilis
recipes.description: Malaysia's national breakfast: rice cooked in coconut milk with pandan and ginger, served with a sweet-hot sambal of dried anchovies, crisp fried anchovies and peanuts, boiled egg and cucumber.

ingredients.name: Palm sugar (gula melaka) or brown sugar
Oil, for frying the anchovies and peanuts

steps.t: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and drain. Put it in the saucepan with the coconut milk, water, salt, ginger, lemongrass and pandan, if using. Bring to the boil, stir once, then cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes. Leave covered off the heat for 10 minutes, then fluff with a fork and remove the aromatics.

Soak the dried chillies in just-boiled water for 15 minutes. Toast the belacan in a dry pan or wrapped in foil for 1–2 minutes until it smells strong and crumbly. Drain the chillies and blend them with the chopped shallots, garlic and belacan and 3 tablespoons of water to a smooth red paste.

Heat the 200 ml of frying oil in the wok to about 170 °C. Fry the peanuts for 3–4 minutes, stirring, until golden, then lift them out. Fry the anchovies for 2–3 minutes until golden and crisp, and lift them out too; they keep crisping as they cool. Pour the oil out of the wok.

Heat the 3 tablespoons of oil in the wok over medium-low heat and fry the chilli paste, stirring often, for 12–15 minutes. It is ready when it has turned a deep brick red, smells sweet rather than raw and the oil separates and floats on top; Malay cooks call this pecah minyak, 'the oil splits'.

Add the sliced shallots and cook for 2 minutes, then the tamarind water, palm sugar and salt. Simmer for 5 minutes until thick and glossy. Stir in half of the fried anchovies and taste: sweet, hot, tangy and salty.
Meanwhile, lower the eggs into boiling water and cook for 9 minutes for firm yolks, then cool in cold water, peel and halve.

Serve each plate with a mound of coconut rice, a spoonful of sambal, the remaining crisp anchovies, the peanuts, half an egg or two and slices of cucumber. In Malaysia it is often wrapped in a banana leaf and newspaper as a takeaway breakfast.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the rice within 1 hour and eat within 2 days. The sambal keeps in a clean jar in the fridge for a week; keep anchovies and peanuts in an airtight jar.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the rice until steaming hot, covered, with a splash of water.
notes: Fried chicken (ayam goreng) or chicken rendang turn nasi lemak into a hearty lunch.

recipes.name: Curry laksa (curry mee)
recipes.description: Kuala Lumpur's spicy coconut curry noodle soup: a rempah of chillies, lemongrass and galangal fried until fragrant, simmered with stock and coconut milk, poured over egg noodles and vermicelli with chicken, prawns, tofu and bean sprouts.

ingredients.name: Tofu puffs (tau pok) or firm tofu
Yellow egg noodles, dried (or 350 g fresh)
Sambal or sliced red chillies, to serve

steps.t: Drain the soaked chillies and dried shrimp. Blend them with the shallots, garlic, lemongrass, galangal, turmeric, toasted coriander, candlenuts and belacan, adding 3–4 tablespoons of water, to a very smooth paste. A smooth rempah fries evenly and gives a silky broth.
Bring the stock to a simmer in the large pot, add the chicken breast and poach gently for 12–15 minutes until cooked through (74 °C in the centre). Lift it out, cool and shred it. Keep the stock.

Heat the oil in the small frying pan or a second pot over medium-low heat. Add the rempah and fry, stirring often, for 10–12 minutes until it darkens, smells fragrant rather than raw and the oil separates out. Stir in the curry powder for the last minute.

Scrape the rempah into the stock and simmer for 10 minutes. Add the coconut milk, palm sugar, salt and tofu puffs and bring back to a gentle simmer; the tofu soaks up the broth like a sponge. Add the prawns and cook for 2–3 minutes until pink.

Meanwhile, cook the egg noodles and the vermicelli in a pan of boiling water according to the packets (usually 3–4 minutes), adding the bean sprouts for the last 20 seconds. Drain and divide between four large bowls.
Taste the broth: it should be rich, spicy and well salted with a gentle sweetness. Adjust with salt or sugar.

Top the noodles with shredded chicken, prawns, tofu puffs and egg halves and ladle over plenty of hot broth. Finish with mint and serve with lime and sambal on the side; a squeeze of lime lifts the richness.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the broth within 2 hours for up to 3 days; store noodles and toppings separately.
recipes.reheating: Bring the broth back to a simmer before ladling over freshly blanched noodles.
notes: Laksa paste from a good brand (about 6 tablespoons) can replace the rempah; fry it for 3–4 minutes.

recipes.name: Penang asam laksa (sour fish noodle soup)
recipes.description: Penang's famous sour, spicy noodle soup: a mackerel broth soured with tamarind and fragrant with lemongrass, laksa leaf and torch ginger, over thick rice noodles with pineapple, cucumber, onion and a spoonful of sweet black prawn paste.

ingredients.name: Asam keping (dried garcinia slices, 3–4), or extra tamarind
Laksa leaves (daun kesum) or Vietnamese mint
Thick round rice noodles (laksa noodles), dried
Hae ko (black prawn paste), thinned with a little hot water

steps.t: Bring the water to the boil in the large pot, add the mackerel and simmer for 10 minutes until the flesh flakes from the bone. Lift out the fish and leave to cool. Keep the broth.

Flake the flesh off the bones in chunks, picking out every bone carefully. Return the heads, bones and skin to the broth and simmer for 15 minutes more, then strain and discard them. Set aside about a third of the flaked fish for the topping.

Blend the soaked dried chillies, fresh chillies, shallots, lemongrass, galangal, turmeric and belacan with a splash of the broth to a smooth paste. Asam laksa's rempah is not fried: it goes straight into the broth, which keeps the flavour bright and sharp.

Stir the paste into the broth with the tamarind, asam keping, laksa leaves and torch ginger flower, if using. Simmer gently for 20–25 minutes, then add the remaining two-thirds of the fish, which breaks down and thickens the broth. Season with the sugar and salt.

Taste: asam laksa should be distinctly sour first, then spicy, salty and slightly sweet, with a strong fish and herb perfume. Add more tamarind or sugar to balance. Fish out the asam keping and torch ginger.
Soak the noodles in warm water for 20 minutes, then boil for 8–10 minutes until soft and slippery. Drain, rinse with hot water and divide between four deep bowls.
Ladle the hot broth over the noodles and top with the reserved fish, cucumber, pineapple, onion, lettuce, mint and chilli. Drizzle a spoonful of hae ko over each bowl; stir it in as you eat.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the broth within 2 hours for up to 3 days (it tastes better the next day). Keep the noodles and raw garnishes separate.
recipes.reheating: Bring the broth back to a simmer before serving.
notes: Sardines or tinned sardines in brine are a common shortcut for the mackerel; add them for the last 10 minutes.

recipes.name: Penang char kway teow (wok-fried flat noodles)
recipes.description: Flat rice noodles stir-fried at blistering heat with prawns, egg, bean sprouts and chives in dark soy and chilli paste until smoky with wok hei. Cook one or two portions at a time.

ingredients.name: Flat rice noodles (kway teow), dried, or 400 g fresh
Cockles or small clams, in shell

steps.t: Soak dried noodles in hot tap water for 10–15 minutes until pliable, then drain well. Fresh noodles just need separating. Blend or pound the soaked chillies and the clove of garlic with a spoonful of water to a paste. Mix the soy sauces, sugar and pepper in a cup. If using cockles, blanch them in boiling water for 30 seconds and pick the meat from the shells.
Arrange everything by the stove in the order it goes in. Char kway teow is cooked in under 5 minutes, and the wok must stay as hot as possible, so cook no more than two portions at a time.

Heat the wok over the highest heat until it smokes. Add 2 tablespoons of oil, the chopped garlic and 1 tablespoon of chilli paste and stir for 15 seconds. Add the prawns (and sausage, if using) and toss for 1 minute until the prawns turn pink at the edges.

Add the noodles and sauce and toss vigorously, scooping from the bottom, for 1–2 minutes until the noodles are evenly coloured and slightly charred in places. Smoke and a little sticking are good: that is the wok hei.
Push the noodles to the side, add the last tablespoon of oil to the space and crack in the eggs. Let them set for 20–30 seconds, then scramble and fold through the noodles.
Add the bean sprouts, chives and cockle meat, if using, and toss for 30–45 seconds, just until the sprouts are hot but still crunchy. Serve immediately, with extra chilli paste and lime on the side.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight from the wok. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a very hot wok or pan for 2–3 minutes, tossing, until steaming hot.
notes: Hawkers fry in lard; neutral oil is used here so the dish suits halal and pork-free cooks. Muslim stalls make it with prawns, squid and beef or chicken slices.

recipes.name: Roti canai with dhal curry
recipes.description: Mamak-stall flatbread: an enriched dough stretched paper-thin, folded into flaky layers and griddled until crisp and golden, then scrunched to open the layers and served with a lentil dhal. Makes 8; the dough rests for at least 4 hours.
equipment: Large flat griddle or heavy frying pan

ingredients.name: Vegetable oil, for soaking and stretching

steps.t: Mix the flour and salt in the bowl. Whisk the condensed milk, egg and water together, pour into the flour with the tablespoon of ghee and mix to a soft, slightly sticky dough. Knead on the worktop for 10 minutes until very smooth and elastic: a small piece should stretch thin without tearing.

Divide the dough into 8 equal balls (about 85 g each), tucking the edges underneath so the tops are smooth. Pour the 100 ml of oil into the tray, roll the balls in it to coat, cover with cling film and rest for at least 4 hours at room temperature, or overnight in the fridge (bring back to room temperature for 1 hour). The long rest relaxes the gluten so the dough stretches paper-thin.

For the dhal, simmer the lentils with the water and turmeric for 15 minutes, skimming off any foam, until soft. Add the potato, carrot and aubergine and simmer for 12–15 minutes more until tender, stirring now and then so nothing sticks.

Temper the spices: heat the 2 tablespoons of oil in the small frying pan over medium heat, add the mustard seeds and let them pop, then add the cumin, dried chillies and curry leaves for 20 seconds. Add the onion, garlic and ginger and fry for 5 minutes until golden, stir in the curry powder for 1 minute, then the tomato for 3 minutes. Tip it all into the dhal with the coconut milk, tamarind and salt and simmer for 5 minutes.

Oil the worktop and your hands generously with oil from the tray. Flatten a ball with your palm, then work outwards with your fingertips, pressing and pulling the edges, until it is a translucent sheet about 40 cm across that you can almost read through. A few small holes are fine.

Fold the sheet into a square parcel: fold the top and bottom edges into the middle, then the sides, trapping air and oil between the layers. (For a spiral, gather the sheet into a rope and coil it like a snail, then flatten it slightly.) Repeat with the rest.

Heat the griddle over medium-high heat and add a little ghee. Cook one roti at a time for 2–3 minutes per side, pressing it down gently with a spatula, until puffed, crisp and golden-brown in patches. Lower the heat if it browns before the centre is cooked.

While each roti is still hot, hold it on its edge and push the sides together between your palms a few times, like clapping, to break open the flaky layers. Serve immediately with a bowl of hot dhal, and sambal or chicken curry if you like.

recipes.storage: Roti are best within an hour of cooking. Freeze folded, uncooked roti between sheets of baking paper for up to 1 month and cook from frozen. Refrigerate the dhal within 2 hours and eat within 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp cooked roti in a dry hot pan for 1 minute per side; reheat the dhal until steaming hot.
notes: The same dough makes roti telur: crack an egg onto the stretched sheet before folding.

recipes.name: Rendang daging (Padang beef rendang)
recipes.description: The Minangkabau festive dish: beef simmered for hours in coconut milk with a fresh chilli, galangal and lemongrass paste until the liquid is gone and the meat fries in the released coconut oil, turning dark, dry and intensely spiced.
equipment: Wide heavy wok (kuali) or large heavy pan

steps.t: Blend the shallots, garlic, fresh and soaked chillies, ginger, galangal, turmeric and sliced lemongrass with a splash of the coconut milk to a smooth, bright red paste.

Put the paste, coconut milk, beef, knotted lemongrass, lime leaves, turmeric leaf (if using), cinnamon, star anise, cloves, cardamom, tamarind and salt in the wok. Stir well and bring to the boil over medium-high heat, stirring so the coconut milk doesn't catch.

Lower the heat to medium and simmer uncovered, stirring every 10 minutes, for about 1½ hours. The liquid reduces to a thick, orange, gravy-like sauce: at this stage the dish is called kalio, and in Padang some families stop here.

Keep cooking over medium-low heat, now stirring every few minutes and scraping the bottom, for another 1–1½ hours. The sauce thickens to a paste and the coconut oil separates out, glistening around the meat.

Lower the heat and stir almost constantly for the last 30–45 minutes as the beef fries in the coconut oil. The paste darkens from brick red to deep brown and clings to the meat in a dry, crumbly coating, and the kitchen smells of caramelised coconut. Don't rush this with high heat: the paste burns easily.
Test a piece: it should be tender but hold its shape, with almost no free liquid in the pan. Remove the whole spices and lemongrass and taste for salt.

Rest the rendang for at least 30 minutes before serving with steamed rice; it is even better the next day. In West Sumatra it keeps for days at room temperature because so little moisture remains, but at home keep it in the fridge.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 5 days, or freeze for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Rendang is about patience, not complexity: allow 4 hours and stay close to the pan for the last hour.
For a quicker, wetter kalio, stop after step 3 and serve with plenty of rice to soak up the sauce.

recipes.name: Rendang ayam (Malaysian chicken rendang)
recipes.description: The Malaysian Hari Raya version: bone-in chicken cooked in a fried spice paste and coconut milk, finished with kerisik (pounded toasted coconut), palm sugar and shredded lime leaves. Wetter, sweeter and quicker than Padang beef rendang.
equipment: Mortar and pestle or food processor

steps.t: Blend the shallots, garlic, ginger, galangal, lemongrass, drained chillies and turmeric with 3–4 tablespoons of water to a smooth paste.

Make the kerisik: toast the coconut in the dry frying pan over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, for 6–8 minutes until evenly deep golden brown. Pound it in the mortar or whizz in a food processor while warm until it turns into a damp, oily brown paste. This toasted coconut gives rendang its nutty depth and thickens the sauce.

Heat the oil in the pot over medium heat and fry the cinnamon, star anise, cloves and cardamom for 30 seconds until fragrant. Add the spice paste and fry, stirring often, for 12–15 minutes until it darkens, smells cooked rather than raw and the oil separates out (pecah minyak).

Add the chicken and turn it in the paste for 3–4 minutes. Pour in the coconut milk and water, add the tamarind, bring to the boil, then simmer uncovered over medium-low heat for 30 minutes, stirring every few minutes and turning the chicken.

Stir in the kerisik, palm sugar and salt and cook for 15–20 minutes more, stirring more often as the sauce thickens, until it is dark, thick and clings to the chicken and oil glistens at the edges. The chicken should be tender, with no pink at the bone.

Stir in the shredded lime leaves (and turmeric leaf, if using) and cook for 2 minutes. Taste: savoury, gently sweet and spicy with a citrus lift. Rest for 10 minutes and serve with rice, nasi lemak or ketupat rice cakes.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days, or freeze for up to 3 months.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Bone-in chicken stays juicier through the long simmer; boneless thighs need only 20 minutes in step 4.

recipes.name: Satay ayam with kuah kacang (chicken satay with peanut sauce)
recipes.description: Malaysian street satay: thin pieces of chicken marinated in turmeric, lemongrass and warm spices, threaded on skewers and grilled over charcoal, served with a spicy-sweet peanut sauce, cucumber and onion. The chicken marinates for at least 4 hours.

steps.t: Blend the shallots, garlic, lemongrass, ginger and galangal for the marinade to a paste with the ground spices, sugar, salt and 2 tablespoons of oil. Mix it thoroughly with the chicken, cover and marinate in the fridge for at least 4 hours, or overnight. Keep the trimmed lemongrass tops for basting.

For the sauce, pulse the peanuts in the food processor until coarsely ground, like rough breadcrumbs with some larger pieces. Blend the soaked chillies, shallots, garlic, lemongrass, galangal and belacan, if using, to a smooth paste.

Heat the 4 tablespoons of oil in the saucepan over medium-low heat and fry the chilli paste, stirring, for 8–10 minutes until dark red and the oil separates. Add the peanuts, tamarind, water, palm sugar and salt and simmer gently, stirring often so it doesn't stick, for 15 minutes until thick and spoonable with oil pooling on top. Taste for sweet, salty, sour and hot.
Thread 4–5 pieces of chicken onto each soaked skewer, pressing them together tightly and leaving a handle at one end. Bunch the lemongrass tops together and bash one end to make a brush.

Grill the skewers over hot charcoal (or on a smoking-hot griddle pan) for 8–10 minutes, turning every 2 minutes and dabbing them with the oil using the lemongrass brush, until charred at the edges and cooked through with no pink inside. The sugar caramelises quickly, so keep them moving.
Serve hot with a bowl of warm peanut sauce for dipping and the cucumber and onion chunks on the side. Ketupat or nasi impit (compressed rice cakes) turn satay into a meal.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate cooked satay and the sauce separately within 2 hours and eat within 3 days. The peanut sauce freezes well.
recipes.reheating: Reheat skewers in a hot oven or under the grill for 4–5 minutes until steaming; warm the sauce with a splash of water.
notes: Beef satay (satay daging) uses the same marinade with thinly sliced rump; grill it for 6–8 minutes.

recipes.name: Bubur cha cha (sweet potato and taro in coconut milk)
recipes.description: A Nyonya dessert soup of colourful sweet potato and taro cubes with chewy sago pearls in pandan-scented coconut milk sweetened with palm sugar. Served warm or chilled.
equipment: Steamer or saucepan with a lid

ingredients.name: Sweet potatoes, orange and purple or yellow

steps.t: Steam the sweet potato and taro cubes in separate piles over boiling water, covered, for 12–15 minutes, until a skewer goes in easily but they still hold their shape. Taro must be fully cooked; raw taro irritates the mouth and throat. Steaming rather than boiling keeps the colours separate and the cubes intact.

Bring a small pan of water to a rolling boil, add the sago and cook, stirring, for 8–10 minutes until the pearls are clear with only a tiny white dot. Turn off the heat, cover and leave for 5 minutes until fully clear, then rinse under cold water in the sieve to wash off the starch.

In the medium saucepan, bring the 600 ml of water to a simmer with the pandan leaves, if using, the palm sugar, sugar and salt, stirring until the sugar dissolves. Simmer for 5 minutes so the pandan perfumes the syrup.
Stir in the coconut milk and heat gently until steaming, without boiling, so it stays smooth. Remove the pandan.
Add the sweet potato, taro and sago and heat through for 2–3 minutes, stirring gently. Taste and add a pinch more salt if needed; the salt makes the coconut taste rich.
Serve warm in small bowls, or chill for 2 hours and serve cold, loosening with a little water or coconut milk as it thickens on standing.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Serve chilled, or warm gently until steaming, stirring.
notes: Store the cooked sweet potato, taro and sago separately from the coconut milk if making ahead, so they don't go mushy.

recipes.name: Mee goreng mamak (spicy fried noodles)
recipes.description: Malaysian Indian-Muslim hawker noodles: yellow noodles wok-fried with tofu, potato, egg and greens in a sweet, tangy and spicy sauce of chilli paste, tomato ketchup and soy, finished with lime.

ingredients.name: Yellow egg noodles, dried (or 350 g fresh)
Firm tofu
ingredients.prep: cut into 2 cm cubes, patted dry
