steps.t: Cook the noodles in boiling water for 2–3 minutes until just tender (fresh noodles need only a quick rinse in hot water), drain, rinse under cold water and shake dry. Blend the soaked chillies, garlic and shallots with a spoonful of water to a paste. Mix the sauce ingredients in a cup.

Heat 1½ tablespoons of the oil in the wok over medium-high heat and fry the tofu cubes, turning, for 5–6 minutes until golden and crisp on most sides. Lift them out. Add the potato and fry for 2–3 minutes until lightly crisp, then lift out too.

Add the remaining 2½ tablespoons of oil and the chilli paste and fry over medium heat, stirring, for 2–3 minutes until dark red and fragrant. Add the onion (and prawns or squid, if using) and stir-fry for 1 minute.

Turn the heat to high, push everything aside and crack the eggs into the wok. Scramble them for 30 seconds until half set, then add the noodles and the sauce and toss vigorously for 2 minutes until every strand is coated and glossy red-brown. Mash some of the potato into the noodles as you toss; mamak cooks do this to thicken the sauce.
Add the tofu, tomato, greens and bean sprouts and toss for 1–2 minutes, until the greens wilt and the sprouts are hot but crunchy. Taste and add more soy or chilli sauce if needed.
Pile onto plates and serve with lime or calamansi to squeeze over: the sharp citrus is essential. Add a fried egg on top for mee goreng special.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a hot wok with a splash of water until steaming hot.
notes: Mamak stalls often add squid, prawns or chicken; this tofu and egg version is the everyday vegetarian plate.

recipes.name: Hainanese chicken rice
recipes.description: Singapore's national dish: a whole chicken gently poached and plunged into ice for silky meat and jelly-like skin, served with rice cooked in chicken fat and stock, a sharp chilli-lime sauce, ginger-scallion oil and sweet dark soy.
equipment: Large stock pot with a lid
Saucepan with a lid for rice

ingredients.name: Chicken fat trimmed from the bird, or vegetable oil

steps.t: Pull any loose fat from the chicken's cavity and keep it for the rice. Rub the bird all over with salt to scrub the skin, rinse and pat dry. Put the ginger slices and knotted spring onions inside the cavity.

Bring the water and tablespoon of salt to the boil in the stock pot. Holding the chicken by the wings, dip it into the boiling water and lift it out three times to tighten the skin, then lower it in breast side down. When the water returns to a bare simmer, cover, turn the heat to the lowest setting and poach for 35–40 minutes without letting it bubble. The thickest part of the thigh should reach 74 °C.

Lift the chicken out, draining the cavity back into the pot, and plunge it into the iced water for 10 minutes. The shock firms the skin into a smooth, gelatinous layer and keeps the meat juicy. Drain, rub with the sesame oil and soy sauce and leave to rest. Keep the poaching stock.

For the rice, render the chicken fat in the saucepan over medium heat (or heat the oil) and fry the garlic, ginger and shallots for 2–3 minutes until fragrant and golden. Add the drained rice and stir for 2 minutes until every grain is coated and glossy. Add 650 ml of poaching stock, the salt and pandan, if using, bring to the boil, cover and cook on the lowest heat for 15 minutes, then leave covered off the heat for 10 minutes.

For the chilli sauce, blend the chillies, garlic, ginger, lime juice, sugar and salt with 3 tablespoons of poaching stock to a coarse, bright red sauce. For the ginger-scallion oil, put the grated ginger, spring onions and salt in a heatproof bowl, heat the oil until it shimmers and pour it over; it will sizzle.

Carve the chicken: cut off the legs and wings, then chop through the bone into 3 cm pieces with the cleaver, and slice the breasts off the bone. Arrange on a platter over cucumber slices and drizzle with a little soy and sesame oil.

Serve each plate with a mound of chicken rice, the chicken, cucumber and coriander, small dishes of chilli sauce, ginger-scallion oil and dark soy, and a bowl of the hot poaching stock seasoned with a pinch of salt and spring onions as soup.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate chicken and rice separately within 1 hour and eat within 2 days; the sauces keep for 5 days.
recipes.reheating: Serve leftover chicken cold or at room temperature as in Singapore, or steam until hot through; reheat rice until steaming hot.
notes: The remaining poaching stock makes an excellent base for congee or noodle soup.

recipes.name: Singapore chilli crab
recipes.description: Mud crabs wok-cooked in a thick, sweet, tangy and gently spicy tomato-chilli sauce finished with ribbons of egg, served with soft buns for mopping up every drop.
equipment: Bowls for shells and finger bowls

ingredients.name: Live mud crabs (2 large), or Dungeness or blue swimmer crabs
Fried or steamed mantou buns, or a crusty baguette

steps.t: Buy the crabs live and cook them the same day. Put them in the freezer for 30 minutes to make them sleepy, then kill each quickly by driving a sturdy knife into the centre of the underside. Pull off the top shell, remove the feathery gills and the mouth parts, rinse, and cut each body into quarters. Crack the claws with the back of the cleaver so the sauce gets in.
Blend the chillies, garlic, shallots, ginger and belacan, if using, with 2 tablespoons of water to a coarse paste. Mix the ketchup, chilli sauce, sugar, salt, vinegar and water in a jug.
Heat the oil in the wok over medium heat and fry the paste, stirring, for 4–5 minutes until fragrant and the raw smell of garlic has gone.

Add the crab pieces and toss to coat in the paste for 2 minutes. Pour in the sauce mixture, bring to the boil, cover and cook over medium-high heat for 10–12 minutes, tossing every few minutes, until the shells are bright orange-red and the meat in the thickest claw is white and opaque all through.
Stir the cornflour mixture and add it to the wok, stirring, for 1 minute until the sauce thickens and turns glossy.

Turn off the heat and pour in the beaten eggs in a thin stream around the wok. Wait 15 seconds, then stir gently so the egg sets into soft ribbons through the sauce. Taste for sweet, sour, salty and hot.
Tip onto a large platter, scatter with spring onions and coriander and serve at once with the buns, crab crackers, a bowl for shells and finger bowls. Eating it is gloriously messy.

recipes.storage: Best eaten straight away. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently in the sauce, covered, until the crab is steaming hot throughout.
notes: Frozen cooked crab claws are a quicker option: add them in step 4 and simmer for 5 minutes, just to heat through.

recipes.name: Kaya toast with soft-boiled eggs
recipes.description: The kopitiam breakfast set: thin, crisp toast sandwiched with homemade pandan coconut jam and cold slabs of butter, served with barely set eggs seasoned with soy sauce and white pepper.

ingredients.name: Pandan leaves, knotted (or ¼ tsp pandan extract)

steps.t: Make the caramel for a golden-brown kaya: melt 2 tablespoons of the sugar in the small saucepan over medium heat, swirling, for 3–4 minutes until amber. Off the heat, carefully stir in 2 tablespoons of the coconut cream (it will bubble) until smooth.
Whisk the 2 eggs and the remaining sugar in the heatproof bowl until the sugar dissolves, then whisk in the rest of the coconut cream and the caramel. Add the pandan leaves.

Set the bowl over a pan of barely simmering water without letting it touch the water. Cook, stirring constantly and scraping the sides with the spatula, for 30–40 minutes. The mixture slowly thickens from thin custard to a thick, glossy jam that holds a trail on the spatula. Patience and low heat stop it scrambling; if it turns grainy, whisk hard off the heat.
Remove the pandan and pass the kaya through the sieve for a silky texture. Leave it to cool and thicken further; you should have about 220 g.

For kopitiam soft-boiled eggs, bring a saucepan of water to a full boil, turn off the heat, lower in the eggs, cover and leave for 6–7 minutes. The whites should be just set and milky, the yolks runny. Drain.
Meanwhile, toast the bread until crisp and golden. Spread 4 slices thickly with kaya, top with slabs of cold butter and close with the remaining slices. Cut into fingers.
Crack two eggs into each small dish, season with soy sauce and white pepper, and serve with the toast for dipping, ideally with a cup of strong kopi or teh.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate leftover kaya in a clean jar for up to 1 week.
notes: For the traditional texture, toast the bread over charcoal or under the grill and slice each piece in half horizontally to make extra-thin, crisp halves.

recipes.name: Chai tow kway (fried carrot cake)
recipes.description: Singapore's hawker 'carrot cake', which contains no carrot: a steamed white radish and rice-flour cake, cubed and fried until crusty, then tossed with egg, garlic, preserved radish and spring onions. The cake is best made a day ahead.
equipment: Steamer large enough for the tin

ingredients.name: Eggs
ingredients.prep: beaten with a pinch of salt

steps.t: Put the grated radish and its juices in the frying pan with 100 ml of the water and cook over medium heat, stirring, for 8–10 minutes until soft and translucent and the liquid has mostly evaporated.

Whisk the rice flour, tapioca starch, salt and pepper with the remaining 300 ml of water until smooth. Lower the heat under the radish, pour in the batter and stir constantly for 2–3 minutes until it thickens into a heavy, sticky paste. Par-cooking stops the flour sinking to the bottom while it steams.

Scrape the mixture into the greased tin and smooth the top. Steam over boiling water, covered, for 40–45 minutes, topping up the water as needed, until the cake is firm, set and a skewer comes out clean.
Cool the cake completely, then cover and refrigerate for at least 2 hours, ideally overnight; it firms up enough to cut cleanly. Turn it out and cut into 2 cm cubes.

Heat 3 tablespoons of the oil in the wok or frying pan over medium-high heat. Fry the cubes in a single layer for 8–10 minutes, turning them only every few minutes, until a golden crust forms on several sides. Don't stir too much, or they break.

Push the cubes to the side, add the last tablespoon of oil, the garlic and chai poh and fry for 1 minute until fragrant, then toss through the cake. Pour the beaten eggs evenly over and around the cubes and leave for 1 minute to set.

Cut and flip the egg-coated cake in sections and fry for 2–3 minutes more until crisp and golden on both sides. Season with soy sauce, fish sauce if using, and pepper, toss with the spring onions and serve hot with chilli on the side.

recipes.storage: Keep the unfried radish cake wrapped in the fridge for up to 4 days. Refrigerate fried leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 1 day.
recipes.reheating: Re-fry in a hot pan for 3–4 minutes until crisp and steaming hot.
notes: For the 'black' version, add 2 tablespoons of sweet dark soy sauce in the last step and toss until the cubes are glazed.
Bought plain radish cake (lo bak go) from an Asian grocer is a good shortcut; start at step 5.

recipes.name: Nasi goreng (Indonesian fried rice)
recipes.description: Day-old rice fried with a pounded paste of shallots, garlic, chilli and shrimp paste, glossed with sweet soy and topped with a fried egg, the way it is sold from street carts across Indonesia.
equipment: Mortar and pestle or small blender

ingredients.name: Cold cooked rice, preferably a day old

steps.t: Pound or blend the shallots, garlic, chillies and toasted terasi to a rough paste. Warm the soy sauce and palm sugar in the small saucepan over low heat, stirring, for 1–2 minutes until the sugar melts into a thick, sweet sauce: a homemade kecap manis. (Or use 3 tablespoons of bottled kecap manis instead.)

Fry the eggs first: heat 2 tablespoons of oil in the wok over medium-high heat and fry the eggs for 2–3 minutes, spooning oil over the whites, until the edges are crisp and the whites set; keep the yolks runny or cook them through as you like. Lift out and keep warm.
Add the 2 tablespoons of oil for the rice to the wok and fry the paste over medium heat, stirring, for 2–3 minutes until it darkens slightly and smells sweet rather than sharp.
Turn the heat to high, add the chicken and stir-fry for 3–4 minutes until cooked through and lightly browned.
Add the rice and toss, pressing out any lumps, for 2–3 minutes until it is hot and every grain is coated in the paste. Day-old rice is drier, so it fries rather than steams.

Pour over the kecap manis, light soy and salt and toss for 1–2 minutes more until the rice is evenly caramel-brown, glossy and a little crisp in places. Taste and adjust, then toss in the spring onions.
Pile onto plates, top each with a fried egg and add cucumber and tomato slices on the side, with fried shallots and prawn crackers if you have them.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Prawns, beef or just egg are all common; for nasi goreng kampung add a handful of fried anchovies and water spinach.

recipes.name: Gado-gado (vegetables with peanut sauce)
recipes.description: Jakarta's favourite salad: blanched and raw vegetables, potatoes, fried tofu and tempeh and boiled egg, smothered in a thick, spicy-sweet peanut sauce and topped with crisp fried shallots.

steps.t: Boil the eggs for 9 minutes, cool in cold water and peel. Bring a large pan of salted water to the boil and blanch each vegetable separately until just tender: carrot 3 minutes, beans 2–3 minutes, cabbage 1 minute, spinach and bean sprouts 30 seconds. Lift each batch out into cold water, then drain. Keep the cucumber raw.
Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat and fry the tofu and tempeh slices for 3–4 minutes per side until golden and crisp. Drain on kitchen paper and cut into bite-size pieces.

For the sauce, blend the peanuts, garlic, chillies, kencur, palm sugar, tamarind, soy sauce, salt and terasi (if using) with the water to a coarse purée. Simmer it in the small saucepan over low heat, stirring constantly, for 4–5 minutes until thick enough to coat a spoon and slightly darker. Stir in the lime juice and add water if it is too thick to pour.
Peel and slice the potatoes and halve the eggs. Arrange all the vegetables, potatoes, tofu, tempeh and eggs on a platter or in shallow bowls.

Pour the warm peanut sauce generously over the top just before serving and scatter with fried shallots. Serve with prawn crackers or rice cakes (lontong) if you like; Jakarta street vendors grind the sauce to order in a stone mortar.

recipes.storage: Store the vegetables and sauce separately in the fridge for up to 2 days; the sauce thickens, so loosen it with warm water.
notes: Leave out the egg and terasi for a vegan gado-gado.

recipes.name: Soto ayam (Javanese turmeric chicken soup)
recipes.description: A bright yellow chicken broth fragrant with turmeric, lemongrass, galangal and lime leaves, poured over glass noodles, shredded chicken, cabbage, bean sprouts and egg, with lime and sambal on the side.

ingredients.name: Indonesian bay leaves (daun salam) or bay leaves
Celery stalk with leaves (or Chinese celery)
Red bird's eye chillies, boiled and blended with salt, for sambal
Steamed rice or rice cakes, to serve

steps.t: Put the chicken and water in the stock pot and bring slowly to the boil, skimming off the foam. Lower the heat and simmer gently while you make the paste.

Blend or pound the shallots, garlic, candlenuts, turmeric, ginger, coriander and white pepper to a smooth yellow paste. Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium heat and fry the paste with the lemongrass, galangal, lime leaves and bay leaves, stirring, for 5–6 minutes until it smells fragrant and the oil turns bright yellow.

Scrape the fried paste and aromatics into the pot, rinsing the pan with a ladle of broth so nothing is wasted. Add the salt and sugar and simmer gently, partly covered, for 35–40 minutes until the chicken is very tender.

Meanwhile, fry the sliced shallots in the 3 tablespoons of oil in the small saucepan over medium-low heat, stirring, for 6–8 minutes until golden; drain on kitchen paper. Blanch the bean sprouts for 20 seconds in boiling water.
Lift out the chicken, shred the meat and discard the bones. Taste the broth: it should be savoury, peppery and fragrant, with a strong turmeric colour. Adjust the salt and keep it at a simmer.

Put some glass noodles, cabbage, bean sprouts and shredded chicken in each bowl with half an egg. Ladle over the hot broth and top with celery, spring onions and fried shallots. Serve with lime wedges, sambal and rice or rice cakes on the side.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the broth within 2 hours for up to 3 days; store the noodles and toppings separately.
recipes.reheating: Bring the broth back to a simmer before ladling it over the bowls.

recipes.name: Sayur lodeh (vegetables in coconut milk)
recipes.description: A gentle Javanese vegetable stew of chayote, long beans, aubergine, corn, tofu and tempeh simmered in a turmeric-tinted coconut broth with galangal and bay leaves. Eaten with rice as part of a family meal.

ingredients.name: Indonesian bay leaves (daun salam) or bay leaves
Young green jackfruit in brine, rinsed

steps.t: Blend or pound the shallots, garlic, candlenuts, chilli, turmeric, coriander and terasi, if using, to a smooth paste with a spoonful of water.
Heat the oil in the saucepan over medium heat and fry the paste with the galangal, bay leaves and lemongrass, stirring, for 4–5 minutes until fragrant and the raw shallot smell has gone.
Pour in the water, bring to the boil and add the corn, chayote and tempeh (and jackfruit, if using). Simmer for 8 minutes until the corn is nearly tender.
Add the long beans, aubergine and tofu and simmer for 5 minutes more.

Stir in the coconut milk, palm sugar and salt and add the cabbage. Bring back to a gentle simmer, stirring often and without letting it boil hard, which can split the coconut milk, for 5–7 minutes until all the vegetables are tender.
Taste: the broth should be mild, savoury and lightly sweet. Remove the galangal, bay and lemongrass and serve hot with rice, tempe goreng and sambal.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Leave out the terasi to keep it vegan. Lodeh is often cooked a day ahead for Javanese celebrations, alongside lontong rice cakes and opor ayam.

recipes.name: Perkedel kentang (Indonesian potato fritters)
recipes.description: Soft, savoury potato patties flavoured with fried shallots, celery leaves, nutmeg and white pepper, dipped in egg and fried golden. A favourite side with soto ayam, sayur lodeh and rice.

ingredients.name: Eggs
ingredients.prep: 1 for the mix, 1 beaten for coating

steps.t: Heat the oil in the pan to 170 °C. Fry the potato slices in batches for 6–8 minutes until golden and cooked through; frying rather than boiling gives perkedel their nutty flavour and dry, fluffy texture. Drain on kitchen paper.
Fry the sliced shallots in the same oil for 3–4 minutes until golden and crisp, lift them out and drain. Turn off the heat under the oil but keep it for later.

Mash the warm potatoes until smooth. Crumble in the fried shallots and add the garlic, celery leaves, spring onions, nutmeg, pepper, salt and one egg. Mix well; the mixture should be soft but hold its shape.
With damp hands, shape the mixture into 12 flat patties about 6 cm across and 1.5 cm thick. Chill them for 10 minutes to firm up if they feel soft.

Reheat the oil to 170 °C. Dip each patty in the beaten egg, letting the excess drip off, and fry 4–5 at a time for 2–3 minutes per side, turning once, until deep golden with a lacy egg coating. Drain on kitchen paper.
Serve warm or at room temperature with soto ayam, sayur lodeh, or simply with rice and sambal.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat in a 200 °C oven for 8–10 minutes until hot and crisp.
notes: Some families add a little minced beef or corned beef to the mixture; fry it with the shallots first.

recipes.name: Martabak manis (terang bulan, sweet thick pancake)
recipes.description: Indonesia's night-market sweet: a thick, honeycombed yeasted pancake cooked in a heavy pan, spread with butter, condensed milk, chocolate sprinkles and peanuts, then folded in half. The batter rests for an hour.
equipment: Heavy cast-iron or thick-based frying pan, about 24 cm, with a lid

ingredients.name: Grated cheddar, for the cheese version

steps.t: Whisk the flour, sugar, salt and yeast in the bowl. Whisk the egg into the lukewarm milk, then pour it into the flour and whisk to a smooth, thick batter like double cream. Cover and leave in a warm place for 1 hour, until bubbly and slightly risen.
Stir the bicarbonate of soda mixture into the batter; it will become frothy and lighter. Leave for 5 minutes while you heat the pan.

Heat the heavy pan over medium-low heat for 3–4 minutes until evenly hot; a drop of water should sizzle gently, not spit. Don't grease it. Pour in all the batter and quickly tilt the pan so a thin layer runs up the sides to make a rim.

Cook uncovered for 2–3 minutes until the surface is covered in holes, like a honeycomb. Sprinkle over the 2 tablespoons of sugar, cover with the lid and cook for 6–8 minutes more, until the top is set and no longer wet and the underside is deep golden brown. Lower the heat if it smells of burning.

Slide the pancake onto a board. While it is hot, spread the top generously with most of the butter so it soaks into the holes, then drizzle with condensed milk and scatter with chocolate sprinkles and peanuts (or cheese).
Fold the pancake in half, brush the outside with the remaining butter, and cut into 8 thick wedges. Serve warm.

recipes.storage: Best eaten warm on the day. Wrap leftovers and keep at room temperature for up to 1 day, or refrigerate for 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Warm in a low oven (150 °C) for 5 minutes.
notes: Chocolate and cheese together (martabak coklat keju) is a hugely popular combination.

recipes.name: Tempe goreng (coriander-garlic fried tempeh)
recipes.description: Slices of tempeh soaked in a garlic, coriander and turmeric brine, then fried until golden and crisp outside and nutty inside. An everyday Javanese side for rice, vegetables and sambal.

ingredients.name: Red chilli with soy sauce, for dipping

steps.t: Pound the garlic, coriander seeds, turmeric and salt in the mortar to a paste. Stir it into the warm water in the shallow dish to make a seasoned brine.
Lay the tempeh slices in the brine, turn them to coat and leave for 10 minutes so the seasoning soaks in.

Heat 1 cm of oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat to about 175 °C, until a corner of tempeh sizzles immediately. Lift the slices out of the brine, shake off excess liquid (it spits) and fry in a single layer for 2–3 minutes per side until deep golden and crisp at the edges.
Drain on kitchen paper and serve hot with rice, sayur lodeh or gado-gado, and sambal or sliced chilli in soy sauce for dipping. They soften as they cool but stay delicious.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a hot pan or a 200 °C oven for 5 minutes.
notes: Tofu slices fried the same way make tahu goreng.

recipes.name: Adobong pusit (squid adobo in its ink)
recipes.description: The seafood cousin of chicken adobo: small squid cooked briefly in vinegar, soy, garlic and their own ink, giving an inky-black, tangy, garlicky sauce with tomatoes and a hint of chilli. Eaten with plenty of rice.
equipment: Large frying pan or wok with a lid

ingredients.name: Squid ink (1 sachet), if your squid have small ink sacs

steps.t: Clean the squid: pull the head and tentacles away from the body. Find the silvery ink sac among the innards, pull it off gently without bursting it and put it in a small bowl with 2 tablespoons of the water. Cut the tentacles off just below the eyes and discard the head, beak and innards; pull out the clear quill from the body and rinse everything well.
Leave small squid bodies whole or cut larger ones into 2 cm rings. Crush the ink sacs in their water and push through the sieve to remove any membrane.

Heat the oil in the pan over medium heat and fry the garlic for 1 minute until pale golden, then add the onion and cook for 3 minutes until soft. Add the tomatoes and cook for 3–4 minutes, pressing them, until they collapse.

Pour in the vinegar and bring it to a simmer without stirring for 2 minutes; Filipino cooks leave adobo vinegar undisturbed until it boils so its raw, sharp edge cooks off. Then add the soy sauce, remaining water, ink, bay leaves, pepper and sugar and simmer for 5 minutes until the sauce thickens slightly.

Add the squid and the chillies and cook over medium-high heat for 2–3 minutes, stirring, just until the squid turns opaque and curls. Squid is tender either very briefly cooked or braised for 30 minutes or more; anything in between turns rubbery, so don't leave it longer.

Lift the squid out with a slotted spoon, boil the sauce hard for 2–3 minutes to reduce it to a glossy black glaze, then return the squid and toss to coat. Taste: sour, salty and garlicky, with a sweet edge from the tomato. Serve hot with steamed rice.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat gently in a covered pan just until steaming hot; long reheating toughens the squid.
notes: Frozen cleaned squid works well; use a sachet of squid ink for the colour.

recipes.name: Sinigang na hipon (sour tamarind prawn soup)
recipes.description: The Philippines' favourite sour soup: head-on prawns and vegetables in a clear tamarind broth with tomato, radish, okra, long beans and water spinach, mouth-puckeringly sour and savoury.

ingredients.name: Water, or the second rinsing water from rice

steps.t: Put the water, onion, tomatoes and taro in the pot and bring to the boil. Simmer for 10–12 minutes until the taro is soft and starting to break down at the edges; it gives the broth a little body. Rice-rinsing water (hugas bigas) is the traditional choice and makes it slightly cloudy and silkier.
Add the radish and stir in the tamarind paste. Simmer for 5 minutes until the radish is translucent at the edges.
Add the aubergine, okra, long beans and chillies and cook for 4–5 minutes until just tender but still bright.
Add the prawns and simmer for 2–3 minutes, just until they turn pink and the heads become bright orange. Don't overcook them, or they turn tough and mealy.

Season with the fish sauce and salt, then taste: sinigang should be strongly sour first and well salted. Add more tamarind if you like it sharper. Turn off the heat, add the water spinach and push it under the broth to wilt for 1 minute.
Ladle into bowls and serve hot with steamed rice and a small dish of fish sauce with crushed chilli for dipping the prawns. Suck the heads for their rich juices.

recipes.storage: Best eaten the day it is made. Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Pork ribs (sinigang na baboy) and milkfish (sinigang na bangus) are the other classic versions; fish is added at the prawn stage.

recipes.name: Kare-kare (oxtail and vegetables in peanut sauce)
recipes.description: A Pampanga fiesta dish: beef simmered until falling off the bone, then finished in a thick, golden peanut sauce coloured with annatto and thickened with toasted rice, with aubergine, long beans and bok choy. Served with salty shrimp paste.
equipment: Large heavy pot with a lid

ingredients.name: Oxtail or bone-in beef short ribs

steps.t: Put the beef in the pot, cover with cold water, bring to a hard boil for 5 minutes, then drain and rinse. Return it to the clean pot with the 2.5 litres of water, the halved onion and salt.

Bring to the boil, skim, cover and simmer gently for 2½–3 hours, until the meat is very tender and pulling away from the bone. Skim off as much fat as you can, then lift out the beef and keep the stock; you need about 1 litre.

Toast the rice flour in the dry frying pan over medium-low heat, stirring constantly, for 5–6 minutes until it is the colour of light peanut butter and smells nutty. Tip into a bowl and whisk in 200 ml of the stock until smooth.
Heat the oil in the cleaned pot over medium-low heat and stir in the annatto for 1 minute until the oil turns orange. Add the garlic and onion and cook for 4–5 minutes until soft.

Whisk in the peanut butter, ground peanuts and 800 ml of the stock until smooth, then whisk in the rice flour mixture and the fish sauce. Simmer, stirring often so it doesn't catch, for 8–10 minutes until thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. Return the beef and simmer for 5 minutes. The sauce is meant to be mild and nutty, not salty; the shrimp paste provides the salt at the table.

While the sauce simmers, blanch the aubergine for 3 minutes, the long beans for 2 minutes and the bok choy for 1 minute in boiling salted water, then drain. Arrange them over or around the beef, or simmer them briefly in the sauce.
Serve hot with steamed rice and a small bowl of sautéed bagoong alamang: each mouthful is eaten with a dab of the salty paste.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days; the sauce thickens, so loosen it with water when reheating.
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Beef shank and tripe are also traditional; the pressure cooker cuts the beef simmering time to about 45 minutes.

recipes.name: Lumpiang shanghai (chicken spring rolls)
recipes.description: Thin, crackling Filipino spring rolls filled with a seasoned minced chicken, carrot and water chestnut mixture, the first thing to disappear at any party. Makes about 30 finger-sized rolls.
equipment: Deep pan or wok for frying

ingredients.name: Lumpia (spring roll) wrappers, about 20 cm square (15 sheets)
Sweet chilli sauce or banana ketchup

steps.t: Mix all the filling ingredients thoroughly in the bowl with your hand for 1–2 minutes until sticky. Fry a teaspoon of it in a little oil to taste for seasoning, and adjust before you start rolling.
Cut the wrapper sheets in half to make rectangles and keep them under a damp cloth so they don't dry and crack. Mix the vinegar, garlic and chilli for the dip.

Lay a wrapper with a long side facing you. Spread about 1 tablespoon of filling in a thin log along the near edge, leaving 2 cm free at each end. Roll it up tightly once, fold in the sides, then keep rolling into a pencil-thin cigar. Dab the far edge with water to seal. Thin rolls cook through before the wrapper burns.

Heat the oil in the deep pan to 170 °C. Fry the rolls in batches of 8–10, turning, for 4–5 minutes until deep golden and crisp all over and the filling is cooked through. Check one: the chicken inside should be white, with no pink, and reach 74 °C.
Drain on the wire rack (paper makes the bottoms soggy) and let the oil come back to temperature between batches.
Serve hot, whole or cut in half on the diagonal, with the garlic vinegar and sweet chilli sauce or banana ketchup for dipping.

recipes.storage: Freeze uncooked rolls on a tray, then bag them, for up to 3 months; fry from frozen for 6–7 minutes. Refrigerate fried rolls within 2 hours and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a 200 °C oven for 8–10 minutes until hot through.
notes: Pork is the traditional filling; minced chicken or beef keep it halal-friendly.

recipes.name: Arroz caldo (Filipino chicken and ginger rice porridge)
recipes.description: A soothing rice porridge cooked with chicken and lots of ginger, tinted golden with safflower, and topped with crisp toasted garlic, spring onions, boiled egg and a squeeze of calamansi. Breakfast, merienda or sick-day food.

ingredients.name: Ginger
ingredients.prep: peeled and cut into thin matchsticks

ingredients.name: Chicken pieces, bone-in and skinless (thighs and drumsticks)
Kasubha (safflower), or a pinch of saffron

steps.t: Make the toasted garlic first: fry half the garlic in 1½ tablespoons of the oil in the small frying pan over medium-low heat, stirring, for 3–4 minutes until evenly golden. Tip it, with its oil, into a bowl straight away; it keeps browning in the hot pan.
Heat the remaining oil in the pot over medium heat and cook the onion, the rest of the garlic and the ginger for 3–4 minutes until soft and very fragrant.
Add the chicken and fish sauce and stir for 3–4 minutes until the chicken is lightly coloured on the outside and has absorbed the fish sauce.

Add both rices and stir for 1 minute to coat them, then pour in the stock and water and add the kasubha, if using. Bring to the boil, then lower the heat and simmer, partly covered, for 35–40 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes and scraping the bottom so it doesn't stick, until the rice has broken down into a thick, creamy porridge and the chicken is tender. Add hot water if it gets too thick.
Meanwhile, boil the eggs for 9 minutes, cool in cold water and peel.

Lift out the chicken, shred the meat off the bones and stir it back in, or serve the pieces whole. Taste and add more fish sauce and pepper. The porridge should pour slowly from a ladle; it thickens as it stands.
Ladle into bowls and top each with an egg, a spoonful of toasted garlic and its oil, spring onions and black pepper. Serve with calamansi to squeeze over and extra fish sauce at the table.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days.
recipes.reheating: Reheat with a splash of water or stock, stirring, until steaming hot throughout.

recipes.name: Champorado (chocolate rice porridge)
recipes.description: A Filipino breakfast and rainy-day favourite: glutinous rice simmered with pure cacao tablets and sugar into a thick, glossy chocolate porridge, swirled with evaporated milk.

ingredients.name: Tablea (pure cacao tablets) or dark chocolate (70–85%)

steps.t: Bring the water to the boil in the saucepan, add the rice and stir. Lower the heat and simmer, stirring every few minutes, for 15 minutes until the grains are swollen and soft and the water has turned starchy.
Add the chopped tablea or chocolate and stir until it melts completely and the porridge turns a deep, even brown.

Stir in the sugar and salt and keep simmering over low heat, stirring constantly now as it thickens, for 5–8 minutes, until the rice is completely tender and the porridge is thick and glossy and falls slowly from the spoon. Add a splash of hot water if it gets too stiff.
Taste and add more sugar if you like; pure tablea is quite bitter. The porridge thickens further as it cools.
Ladle into bowls and pour a swirl of evaporated milk over each one. Serve hot, or at room temperature as some families prefer.
For the classic sweet-salty pairing, serve with crisp fried dried fish (tuyo) on the side, or sprinkle with a little sugar and toasted rice for crunch.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate within 2 hours and eat within 3 days; it sets firm when cold.
recipes.reheating: Reheat with a splash of water or milk, stirring, until hot and creamy again.

recipes.name: Turon (caramelised banana and jackfruit spring rolls)
recipes.description: A favourite Filipino merienda: saba bananas and ripe jackfruit rolled in brown sugar and lumpia wrappers, fried until crisp and coated in a shiny, crackly caramel.

ingredients.name: Saba bananas (6), or small ripe plantains

steps.t: Spread 60 g of the brown sugar on a plate. Roll each banana half in the sugar until well coated.

Lay a wrapper on the board with one corner pointing towards you. Put a sugared banana half across the lower part with a strip or two of jackfruit alongside. Fold the bottom corner over, fold in the sides and roll up tightly, sealing the last corner with a dab of water. Repeat with the rest.
Heat 2 cm of oil in the pan to 170 °C. Fry the rolls 4 at a time for 2–3 minutes, turning, until light golden and crisp.

Now caramelise them: sprinkle a tablespoon or two of the remaining brown sugar over the oil around the rolls. It melts, sinks and bubbles up around them; keep turning the rolls with tongs for 1–2 minutes so they pick up a glossy amber coating. Lift them out before the sugar darkens beyond deep amber, or it turns bitter.
Set the turon on a rack or baking paper, not kitchen paper, which would stick to the caramel. Skim any burnt sugar from the oil before the next batch.
Let them cool for 5 minutes so the caramel hardens and crackles, then serve warm. The filling stays very hot, so warn children before they bite.

recipes.storage: Best eaten within a few hours, while the caramel is crisp. Keep leftovers uncovered at room temperature for up to 1 day.
recipes.reheating: Re-crisp in a 180 °C oven for 5 minutes.
notes: Saba are starchy cooking bananas; plantains that are yellow with black spots are the closest substitute. Ripe ordinary bananas are too soft.

recipes.name: Pandesal (Filipino breakfast rolls)
recipes.description: Soft, lightly sweet bread rolls with a crumb-coated crust, sold warm from neighbourhood bakeries every morning. Makes 16 rolls; the dough needs about 2 hours to rise.
equipment: Large mixing bowl or stand mixer
Baking tray lined with baking paper

steps.t: Mix the flour, yeast, sugar and salt in the bowl. Add the milk, water and egg and mix to a shaggy dough, then add the butter and knead for 10–12 minutes by hand (6–8 minutes in a mixer) until smooth, soft and elastic. Stretch a small piece: it should go thin enough to let light through without tearing.
Shape the dough into a ball, put it back in the bowl, cover with the tea towel and leave in a warm place for 1–1½ hours until doubled in size.
Knock the air out and divide the dough in two. Roll each half into a log about 40 cm long and 4 cm thick. Roll the logs in the breadcrumbs to coat them all over.

Cut each log into 8 equal pieces with the bench scraper. Lay them cut side up on the lined tray, 4 cm apart, and press lightly to flatten. Sprinkle with a few more breadcrumbs, cover loosely and leave to rise for 40–45 minutes until puffy.
Heat the oven to 190 °C. Bake the rolls in the centre of the oven for 15–18 minutes, until risen and pale golden and the bottoms sound hollow when tapped.
Cool on a rack for 10 minutes. Pandesal is best eaten warm, split and filled with butter, cheese, coconut jam or fried egg, with a cup of coffee.

recipes.storage: Keep in an airtight bag at room temperature for 2 days, or freeze for up to 1 month.
recipes.reheating: Warm in a 150 °C oven or toaster oven for 3–4 minutes.
notes: The name means 'salt bread', although the rolls are slightly sweet.

recipes.name: Mohinga (Burmese fish and rice noodle soup)
recipes.description: Myanmar's national breakfast: a thick, peppery fish broth fragrant with lemongrass, ginger and turmeric, thickened with toasted rice and chickpea flour and poured over thin rice noodles, with boiled egg, lime and crisp toppings.

ingredients.name: Catfish steaks or fillets (or other firm white fish)
Uncooked rice, for toasted rice powder
Ngapi (Burmese shrimp paste) or other shrimp paste

steps.t: Simmer the fish in the water with the bruised lemongrass and half the turmeric for 12–15 minutes until it flakes easily. Lift out the fish, flake the flesh into chunks and discard skin and bones. Strain and keep the stock.

Toast the rice in a dry frying pan over medium-low heat, stirring, for 6–8 minutes until golden, then grind to a fine powder. In the same pan, toast the chickpea flour, stirring constantly, for 3–4 minutes until it smells nutty and darkens a shade. Whisk both powders with 300 ml of cold water to a smooth paste.

Blend the onions, garlic, ginger and sliced lemongrass to a paste. Heat the oil in the pot over medium heat, add the paste with the remaining turmeric, paprika and chilli powder and fry, stirring, for 10–12 minutes until the water has cooked off, the paste is golden and the oil separates out.

Add the flaked fish and fry gently for 2 minutes, breaking it up a little. Pour in the fish stock and the rice and chickpea paste, stirring constantly so it doesn't go lumpy, then add the whole shallots, fish sauce, shrimp paste and pepper.

Simmer gently, stirring often, for 20–25 minutes until the shallots are soft and the soup is thick enough to coat a spoon, like a light gravy. Add water if it gets too thick. Taste: it should be peppery, savoury and rich with fish. Add more fish sauce or pepper as needed.
Meanwhile, cook the noodles as the packet directs (usually 3–4 minutes), rinse briefly and drain. Divide between six bowls.
Ladle the hot soup over the noodles and top with egg halves and coriander. Serve with lime wedges and chilli flakes, and crisp split-pea or chickpea-flour fritters to crumble over if you have them.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate the soup within 2 hours for up to 3 days; store the noodles separately.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the soup with a splash of water, stirring, until steaming hot.
notes: Sliced banana stem, simmered with the shallots, is traditional and adds a crisp, slightly sweet bite.
Tinned mackerel or sardines in brine are a common shortcut for the fresh fish.

recipes.name: Kyet thar hin (Burmese chicken curry)
recipes.description: An everyday Burmese curry: chicken cooked in a slow-fried paste of onion, garlic and ginger with turmeric and paprika until the oil rises to the top, glossy red and mellow rather than fiery. Eaten with rice and a sour soup.

steps.t: Rub the chicken with half the turmeric, the fish sauce and half the salt and leave for 15 minutes while you make the paste.
Blend the onions, garlic and ginger to a coarse purée, or grate them on the box grater.

Heat the oil in the pot over medium heat and fry the cinnamon, cardamom and bay leaves for 30 seconds. Add the onion purée with the remaining turmeric and cook, stirring often, for 15–20 minutes. The water cooks off first, then the paste fries in the oil, turning from pale to deep golden and smelling sweet. Lower the heat if it sticks; this slow frying is what gives Burmese curries their mellow depth.
Stir in the paprika, chilli powder and garam masala for 30 seconds, then add the tomato and cook for 3 minutes until it breaks down.

Add the chicken and turn it in the paste for 3–4 minutes until coated and lightly sealed. Pour in the water and the remaining salt, bring to the boil, cover and simmer over low heat for 25 minutes, stirring once or twice.

Uncover and cook for 5–10 minutes more until the sauce has reduced and the oil has separated and floats in a red layer on top (Burmese cooks call this si pyan, 'the oil returns'). The chicken should be tender with no pink at the bone. Taste for salt.
Scatter with coriander and serve with plenty of steamed rice, a clear sour soup and raw or blanched vegetables with a chilli dip. Spoon off some of the oil before serving if you prefer it lighter.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Add halved potatoes with the water to make kyet thar aloo hin.

recipes.name: To hpu thoke (Shan tofu salad)
recipes.description: Shan State's golden 'tofu' made not from soy but from chickpea flour, set and cut into strips, then dressed with garlic oil, chilli oil, soy, tamarind, crunchy peanuts and fresh coriander. The tofu needs about 2 hours to set.

steps.t: Whisk the chickpea flour, turmeric and salt with 250 ml of the water to a smooth, lump-free batter. Bring the remaining 450 ml of water to the boil in the saucepan, then lower the heat to medium and pour in the batter in a thin stream, whisking constantly.

Switch to the wooden spoon and keep stirring without stopping for 8–10 minutes as it thickens, bubbles and turns glossy, until it is very thick and pulls away from the base of the pan, like stiff polenta. Undercooked batter tastes raw and won't set.
Pour it straight into the oiled dish, smooth the top and leave to cool and set for 2 hours at room temperature (or 1 hour in the fridge) until firm enough to slice like a soft jelly.

For the garlic oil, fry the sliced garlic in the 3 tablespoons of oil over medium-low heat for 3–4 minutes until golden, then scoop out the garlic and keep the oil. Heat the extra tablespoon of oil until hot, pour it over the chilli flakes in a heatproof bowl and stir.
Turn the set tofu out and cut it into 1 cm strips or bite-size triangles. Put them in a wide bowl with the shallots and cabbage.

Add 2 tablespoons of garlic oil, chilli oil to taste, the soy sauce, tamarind water, lime juice and sugar and toss gently with your hands so the tofu doesn't break. Taste: tangy, nutty, garlicky and gently hot. Top with the fried garlic, peanuts, sesame and coriander and serve at room temperature.

recipes.storage: Keep the unsliced Shan tofu covered in the fridge for up to 3 days; dress just before serving.
notes: The same tofu is cut into thick slices and deep-fried to make crisp tohu jaw fritters, eaten with a tamarind dip.

recipes.name: Amok trey (Cambodian steamed fish curry)
recipes.description: Cambodia's best-known dish: chunks of white fish folded into a silky coconut custard flavoured with kroeung, a fresh lemongrass, galangal and turmeric paste, then steamed in banana-leaf cups on a bed of greens.
equipment: Banana leaves and toothpicks, or 4 ramekins

ingredients.name: Makrut lime leaves (plus the zest of 1 makrut lime, if you have it)
Firm white fish fillets (snapper, catfish or cod)
Noni leaves (slek ngor), or young spinach or cabbage leaves

steps.t: Pound the kroeung in the mortar, starting with the lemongrass, galangal and fingerroot and adding the lime leaves, garlic, shallots, chillies, turmeric and shrimp paste a little at a time, for 10–15 minutes until you have a fine, damp yellow paste. A blender works with a splash of the coconut cream; scrape down often.

Make 4 banana-leaf cups: soften the leaves by passing them briefly over a flame or dipping them in hot water, cut two 20 cm circles for each cup, stack them and pinch four corners up into a square bowl, securing each fold with a toothpick. Ramekins work too.
Whisk 250 ml of the coconut cream with the kroeung, egg, fish sauce, palm sugar and salt until smooth, then fold in the fish. Leave for 10 minutes so the fish takes on the flavours.
Line each cup with a layer of the noni or spinach leaves, then spoon in the fish mixture, filling them to just below the rim.

Set the cups in the steamer over simmering water, cover and steam for 18–20 minutes, until the custard is just set and wobbles slightly in the centre and the fish is opaque throughout. Keep the heat moderate: fierce steam makes the custard curdle and weep.
Spoon the remaining coconut cream over the tops and steam for 2 minutes more to set it into a glossy white layer.
Scatter with shredded lime leaves and chilli slivers and serve hot in the cups with steamed jasmine rice.

recipes.storage: Best eaten freshly steamed. Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 2 days.
recipes.reheating: Re-steam for 8–10 minutes until hot through.
notes: Thai hor mok pla is a close relative; Cambodian amok is milder, thicker and more fragrant with turmeric and lemongrass.

recipes.name: Beef lok lak with lime-pepper dip
recipes.description: Cubes of beef marinated in oyster sauce, soy and garlic and seared fast in a hot wok, served over lettuce, tomato and onion with teuk meric, a sharp dipping sauce of lime juice and Kampot black pepper.
equipment: Wok or large heavy frying pan

ingredients.name: Black pepper, freshly and coarsely ground (Kampot if possible)

steps.t: Mix the beef with the oyster sauce, soy sauce, fish sauce, ketchup, sugar, garlic, pepper and cornflour and leave to marinate for 15–30 minutes while you prepare everything else.
For the teuk meric, stir the lime juice, coarse pepper, salt and sugar together in small bowls, one per person, until the salt and sugar dissolve. It should be sharp, peppery and salty.
Arrange the lettuce, tomatoes, onion and cucumber on four plates.

Heat the wok over high heat until it smokes and add the oil. Lift the beef out of any marinade pooled in the bowl and add it in a single layer, in two batches if your wok is small; crowding the pan makes the beef stew grey instead of searing. Leave it untouched for 1 minute until a dark crust forms underneath.

Toss the beef for 2–3 minutes more, adding the last of the marinade for the final 30 seconds, until it is browned and glazed outside and still pink in the centre (cook it longer if you prefer it well done). Lift it out straight away so it doesn't overcook in the hot wok.
Spoon the beef and its glossy sauce over the salad, top with a fried egg if you like, and serve with steamed rice and the lime-pepper dip. Dip each piece of beef before eating.

recipes.storage: Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours and eat within 2 days; the salad is best fresh.
recipes.reheating: Reheat the beef quickly in a hot pan until steaming.
notes: Cambodian lok lak is often served with rice cooked with a little tomato paste; Vietnamese bò lúc lắc is its close cousin.

recipes.name: Gaeng keow wan pak (green curry with tofu and vegetables)
recipes.description: A meat-free Thai green curry: a fresh paste of green chillies, lemongrass, galangal and coriander fried in coconut cream, simmered with tofu, Thai aubergine and bamboo shoots, seasoned with soy sauce instead of fish sauce and finished with Thai basil.

ingredients.name: Green bird's eye or long green chillies

steps.t: Pound or blend all the paste ingredients, adding 1–2 tablespoons of water if blending, for several minutes until you have a fine, bright green paste with no fibrous bits of lemongrass. Scrape down the sides often.
Pat the tofu dry. Heat the oil in the frying pan over medium-high heat and fry the cubes, turning, for 5–6 minutes until golden on most sides; this helps them keep their shape in the curry.

Spoon about 5 tablespoons of the thick cream from the top of the coconut milk into the wok and heat over medium heat until it bubbles and the oil separates. Add the paste and fry, stirring, for 3–4 minutes until intensely fragrant and the oil turns green.

Pour in the rest of the coconut milk and the stock, add the aubergine and simmer for 5 minutes. Add the bamboo shoots, beans, tofu, soy sauce, palm sugar and torn lime leaves and simmer for 4–5 minutes more until the vegetables are just tender.
Taste: green curry should be hot and herbal first, then rich, salty and faintly sweet. Add more soy for salt or sugar to round off the heat.
Take it off the heat, stir in the basil and sliced chilli and let the basil wilt for a few seconds. Serve with jasmine rice.

recipes.storage: @fridge3
recipes.reheating: @reheat
notes: Check the label if you use a store-bought paste: most contain shrimp paste, so look for a vegetarian one (about 3 tablespoons).
